items.title: Nvidia Allegedly Engineered Scarcity by Funding AI Startups to Buy Its GPUs
items.author: speckx
items.content:
Following the departure of now-former NVIDIA CEO, Jensen Huang, a new report by The Wall Street Journal (via Wccftech) has emerged alleging that NVIDIA artificially inflated the ongoing GPU and memory shortage by investing in AI startups that would go on to buy NVIDIA GPUs and build data centers. The reason behind this was to maintain the perception of ongoing high demand and to move an oversupply of semiconductors from TSMC.

The WSJ report cites an August meeting between Huang and his senior finance team, including NVIDIA's CFO and acting CEO, Colette Kress, during which Kress pushed for a reduction in circular financing agreements, in response to which Huang allegedly lay into Kress, calling her a "deer in the headlights," after she had pushed to scale back

NVIDIA's $250 billion deal with OpenAI. Jensen's push for further investment into small-scale cloud providers was seemingly in response to the changing tide that saw AI hyperscalers move away from off-the-shelf components in favor of custom solutions.The situation described in the report saw NVIDIA on the hook for an "avalanche" of GPUs from TSMC, for which it would have no immediate buyers. Part of the issue highlighted by Kress was also that these small-scale cloud providers NVIDIA was investing in could not afford to buy NVIDIA GPUs, meaning they, too, could be a financial dead end.

items.title: Amtrak booking system experiencing major issues amid nationwide FAA ground stop
items.author: snow_mac
items.content:
Amtrak said its booking system is returning to normal after a network outage that coincided with a nationwide FAA ground stop.

Users on social media started sharing frustrations over ticket reservations Friday afternoon, with travelers showing error messages on Amtrak's website and app.

Hundreds of users reported issues on DownDetector, beginning shortly before 5 p.m. Friday, with another surge just before 6 p.m.

Issues caused by increased demand

In response to a request for comment, Amtrak's Communications Director W. Kyle Anderson said that "Amtrak service is operating normally, and we are seeing increased demand for travel across our network."

Responding to a frustrated customer Friday, Amtrak officials said in a post on X that the booking issues were related to a system-wide update, but did not elaborate.

Around 9 p.m. officials said the booking systems were returning to normal. 

The company said some customers may still experience issues while processing payments, booking trips or modifying existing reservations. Amtrak’s call centers experienced higher-than-normal call volumes, resulting in longer wait times for some.

FOX 5 DC attempted to call the support number during the outage, around 8 p.m., but an automated message said officials were unable to take calls due to "unusually high call volume."

Travelers scrambling during ground stop

The outage came as thousands of travelers across the country scrambled for new plans, after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop — the first since January 2023 and just the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

The FAA has said that the ground stop was ordered due to a "temporary telecommunications outage." It has since been lifted. 

Information in this story is from social media posts commenting on the ticket booking outage, error messages on Amtrak's website and app, phone calls to Amtrak's support and media relations lines and previous FOX reporting on the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop.

items.title: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
items.author: vinhnx
items.content:
This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.

I maintain Ratatui, so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.

Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough by hand to have opinions about this.

The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:

So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.

Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.

Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:

Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.

  • Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side.
  • Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top.
  • Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge.
  • Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text.
  • Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it.

The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback:

The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame:

Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui:

And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines:

Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog:

Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here:

The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that.

Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration.

You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included.

Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box (pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never get copied, which cuts both ways.

A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors.

The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters ( and friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better way to do that part. One problem at a time.

The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them.

Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it.

When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The stroke with the higher wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below. That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor.

Everything is one DCS string with a namespace:

The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders:

There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives without a reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it, the same as any unknown DCS.

The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope.

Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible.

The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the in ). That's v1 in the old sense, before we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer.

Parts of this have been done before:

  • in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color.
  • : framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge.
  • The has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. and (, and friends) have similar attributes. These are the closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves.
  • terminals can outline whole input fields.

What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol.

My own first prototype was in Rio (raphamorim/rio#1947), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that.

When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed.

Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.

Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.

Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.

On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.

Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.

The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode):

Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation:

Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: placement, colors, blocks, junctions, halves, styles and live. cycles the stroke width, turns borders off so you can compare, and quits. Each view also has a matching flag (, and so on) if you want to start on it.

The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch. It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above:

Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. and split, closes, and right click opens a pane menu. Press to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or to shade alternate cells and see where the edges are.

The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop:

It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. to show and hide the boxes, and work the same as in the panes demo, and or lists the rest of the keys. It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the dependency.

I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion.

items.title: Live-migration support in FreeBSD and bhyve coming
items.author: JohnDohnBohn
items.content:
This project presents a first working state for live migration of bhyve guests on FreeBSD 15.1. A running amd64 guest can move between two hosts over TCP while continuing to run; it is paused only for the final stop-and-copy phase. The work builds on bhyve's experimental snapshot support and adds dirty-page tracking in the vmm kernel module together with a migration protocol in bhyve and bhyvectl.

The goal is deliberately practical: make it possible to test, discuss, and improve a real implementation rather than discuss live migration only in the abstract. The current code and test tooling are being published as a WIP RFC so that the next steps can be shaped in the open. A more detailed demonstration of a VM being live migrated can be watched on my YouTube channel.

Live migration is an important building block for enterprise virtualisation. It enables host maintenance, hardware replacement, load balancing, and failure-domain management with far less disruption to workloads. It is also central to the Sylve project, which aims to offer a Proxmox-like virtualisation solution for FreeBSD. Migration is not an optional convenience in that kind of platform; it is one of the capabilities that makes clustered operations practical.

It is equally important for BoxyBSD, where I offer free BSD-based VPS instances to individuals. Without a credible migration path, routine host work can require a guest outage. That makes live migration a current show stopper for the project, and is why this work is being pushed toward a testable, reviewable state.

How the current implementation works

The source starts with a pre-copy phase. It sends populated guest memory, then repeatedly obtains a bitmap of pages changed since the previous scan and sends only those pages. Once the remaining dirty set fits the configured downtime target, stops shrinking, or reaches the configured round limit, bhyve pauses the guest and its devices. It then sends the final dirty pages and the existing snapshot state for the vCPUs, kernel state, and emulated devices.

The destination validates the basic VM geometry, receives memory and state, restores it, and reports that it is ready. Only then does the source send , the commit point. Before , a failed migration can resume the source guest. The destination does not start the guest if it does not receive that commit message. A warm, stop-and-copy mode is available too, which is useful both as a fallback and as a comparison baseline.

What is implemented today

  • Pre-copy and warm migration: live pre-copy is configurable with downtime and maximum-round controls; explicit stop-and-copy migration is also supported.
  • Multi-vCPU protocol support: the migration handshake carries the guest vCPU count, the destination refuses a count mismatch, and all guest vCPUs are paused and resumed as part of migration. The published test bed has primarily exercised a one-vCPU guest, so multi-vCPU stress and race testing remain required before making broader claims.
  • Memory consistency checks: dirty-page tracking covers guest and mapped emulation writes through page dirty state, while vmm write holds are recorded separately. The test workload rewrites and verifies guest memory and reports any missing or stale page as a mismatch. Repeated ping-pong migrations have been used to check that the workload continues without errors.
  • a guest-side workload repeatedly writes and fsyncs files, verifies checksums, and is checked again after a cold reboot. This is intended to exercise the device pause, drain, and restore path.
  • destination refusal, an unreachable target, and a target disappearing during both pre-copy and stop-and-copy have been tested. Before commit, the source is intended to resume the paused guest after failure.
  • Basic destination checks: protocol version, page size, memory layout, and vCPU count are checked before data transfer. The migration socket is opened by bhyvectl and passed into bhyve so that bhyve can remain inside its Capsicum sandbox.
  • this is amd64-only and depends on the experimental support. It relies on snapshot-capable emulated devices; PCI passthrough is not migratablem, yet.

In the current two-host test environment, repeated live migrations, memory-rewrite workloads, and fsync-heavy disk workloads have completed successfully. For a slowly dirtying 512 MiB guest, observed downtime has been roughly 138–171 ms. A rapidly dirtying guest may not converge during pre-copy, but still falls back to a correct stop-and-copy completion with a longer pause. These are encouraging engineering results, not a production support promise or a complete correctness proof.

Blockers before upstreaming can be evaluated further

The following are neutral engineering requirements, not criticism of the value of the prototype. They need to be addressed first before further upstreaming into FreeBSD can be evaluated responsibly.

  • Prove and harden dirty-log correctness. The kernel-side dirty-page algorithm must be demonstrated not to lose a write while dirty bits are examined and cleared. It needs focused concurrency, paging, emulation-write, and multi-vCPU stress coverage, plus a reviewable locking and memory-ordering argument.
  • Define a complete compatibility contract. Matching memory size and vCPU count is not enough. A destination should verify guest identity, CPU capabilities, bhyve/vmm and snapshot format compatibility, device topology and capabilities, and shared-storage identity before accepting a migration.
  • Harden the transport and protocol. The current TCP transport has no authentication or encryption and uses a first-version native protocol. A stable protocol needs explicit wire formats, bounded message handling, timeouts, version negotiation, authentication or a supported external secure transport model, and clear operational guidance.
  • Clarify the commit and device-side-effect boundary. The source/destination handoff must be reviewed so that device restoration cannot cause externally visible work before the source has committed, and so that the unavoidable uncertain outcome after a lost post-commit acknowledgement is operationally recoverable.
  • Specify storage and network handoff. Shared storage must have defined coherency, durability, and fencing assumptions. Network migration also needs a clear answer for tap/bridge handling, MAC/IP movement, and traffic convergence.
  • Build an in-tree test strategy. The current scripts and test-bed workloads are useful, but upstream review will need automated regression coverage and a documented support matrix across CPU counts, memory sizes, supported devices, host CPUs, and failure cases.
  • Separate the work into reviewable patches. Dirty-page tracking, snapshot API refactoring, protocol/receiver work, CLI changes, and tests should be independently reviewable. This will make design feedback more actionable and reduce the risk of merging coupled changes.

We have already had deeper discussions about these questions in the Sylve Discord. Publishing this current state is intended to make those discussions more concrete, bring in wider FreeBSD and bhyve feedback, and turn the prototype into a clear roadmap. The immediate focus is correctness, compatibility validation, transport safety, and repeatable tests—not adding performance features first. Currently, some peopel already have access to it and it's planned ot publish this at least as a proposal on my git and GitHub at:

Compression, zero-page elision, broader device coverage, richer orchestration, and performance tuning can follow once the foundation is sound. If you operate bhyve, work on FreeBSD virtualisation, or are interested in Sylve or BoxyBSD, testing the RFC and contributing design feedback would be especially valuable.

  1. 实机把 MASTER 放在适中的位置；网页点琴键或播放即可发声，无需额外开关。

  6. 按 SAVE，SELECT 选 USER 槽，再按 SAVE 保存；覆盖其他已有槽会提示确认，成功后自动返回。

网页顶部“保存到设备”可直接选槽保存；“存到此浏览器”只存本机浏览器；“导出项目文件”生成电脑备份。实机 SAVE 保存到设备槽。

从编辑页回八轨总览；已经在总览时打开预设，再按取消。
总览、常用音色、步进和混音页选轨；完整细调页翻参数页；菜单选项目。

同一轨的静音与独奏互斥：开启独奏会取消该轨静音，开启静音会取消该轨独奏；其他轨保持原状态。

选择预设后点“播放”试听。“读取与保存”管理设备读取和浏览器存档，“文件与 MIDI”导入、导出项目和音色。

常用编辑按钮直接打开音色、步进、混音和效果；其余功能在“更多编辑”。旋钮可拖动或滚轮调节，LCD 数值可点击编辑。电脑键盘 Z、S、X、D…演奏，空格播放，Esc 停音；输入文字和操作菜单时不会演奏。

上排功能键在所有页面都有效：FX、SCL、ENV、LFO、EDIT、GLO、SEQ 可直接切页，ARP 短按开关、长按调参数，PLAY 控制播放。菜单或步进细节中按 REC，会进入 SEQ 基础页并开始录入；再按结束。SAVE 打开项目保存页，或执行屏幕内的确认；OCT−／OCT+ 在 SEQ 和复制菜单翻步进页，其他页面调八度。离开确认页不会执行待确认操作。

把鼠标放在 LCD 上的数值，出现高亮即可滚轮调节；每次按参数最小步长变化，不随滚动速度加速。也可点击打开大号数值框，用滚轮、＋／−或方向键细调，Esc 关闭。支持底部参数、顶部 BPM、总览各轨音量、SEQ 循环长度、步进详情的选步数字、音色参数行、效果参数行，以及 FM 的 ALG、FB、MONO／POLY、ADSR 开关、LFO 波形／同步／PM SENS。混音页也可点静音／独奏格子设置。状态、电平、固定量化和当前引擎不支持的参数只显示；外部 MIDI 时钟下 BPM 由外部控制。切换轨道或参数页会关闭旧编辑框，避免改错参数。总览调其他轨的小音量数字不会改变当前选轨。

GLO 短按（小于 0.6 秒）进入或退出混音；按住 0.6 秒可临时查看混音，松开回原页。GLO、EDIT、SEQ、ARP 的长按过程中，屏幕顶部显示进度条。

HOME＋PLAY 紧急停音回起点；HOME＋SAVE 撤销／重做；SEQ＋EDIT 打开更多菜单；EDIT＋REC 改 DX7 音色名。都可以从长按 SEQ 的菜单完成对应操作。网页需要锁住按键时可 Shift 点击或右击，再点释放；日常操作无需使用。

SEQ 基础页白键开关当前页的步；K3 选音高或鼓声部。PRESETS 在各参数页统一选步，SELECT 选轨，OCT−／OCT+ 每次换 16 步。ALGORITHM 翻底部八页：BASIC、STEP DETAILS、RHYTHM/REC、LOCKS、SYNC / LOOP、MIDI TRACK、MIDI ROUTING、TRACK ROLE。RHYTHM/REC 的 K4 选本轨 16／32／48／64 步，各轨独立循环。

播放中修改长度会显示 ，到本轨下一轮起点生效。缩短不会删除后面的音符，再加长即可恢复。屏幕 表示跟随播放翻页；手动编辑后显示 并固定页面，再按 SEQ 返回基础页并恢复跟随。

SEQ 基础页：旋律轨 K2 选步，K3 改已有音符；空步只设待输入音高，按白键写入。鼓轨 K3 选声部，不移动鼓点。K1 调轨道音量，K4 调速度；外部 MIDI 时钟下速度由外部设备控制。

SEQ 的 SYNC / LOOP 页：K1 选 INT／MIDI，K2 调内部 BPM，K3 调循环长度。切换时钟会停止播放；MIDI 模式需外部 Start／Continue 和 Clock，等待时屏幕提示 WAIT MIDI CLOCK。外部 BPM 只读，蓝牙页的时钟设置仍可使用。

SEQ 的 MIDI TRACK 页：K1 选 SEQ／ARP 的 LOCAL／BOTH／MIDI 输出，K2 选输出通道，K3 选端口，K4 开关 KEY OUT。MIDI ROUTING 页：K1 为 LOCAL，K2 为 CLK OUT，K3 选 THRU IN，K4 选 THRU OUT。SYNC 页 K4 选时钟来源。这些偏好独立于工程；网页仅预览，不向实际 MIDI 端口外发，实机请通过机身设置。

录入标记：停止时按 REC 显示 STEP，弹琴逐步写入；播放时显示 REC，按时间录入；启用预备拍后显示 CNT 4→1，下一小节才开始记录。绿色短线表示播放步，白色框表示编辑步；PRESETS 手动选步会结束录入，再按 REC 继续。

短按 ARP 开启后按住音符；长按 ARP 打开参数。ALGORITHM 翻两页：第一页 K1 为 1/4、1/8、1/16、1/32 分频，K2 方向，K3 为 1–4 个八度，K4 为 25%–100% 门长；第二页 K1 为 0%–50% Swing，K2 开关 Hold。Hold 保持松手后的和弦，全部松手后弹新和弦即可替换；关闭 Hold、停止或紧急停音会释放锁住的音符。SELECT 选轨，各轨参数独立。HOME／SEQ 基础页 K4 调 BPM；外部时钟需 Start／Continue 和 Clock，Swing 按 24 PPQN 的精度变化。

808／SAMPLER 支持分频、方向、Swing 和 Hold；音域与门长显示“--”，不移调鼓声部。ARP 开关与六项参数随项目保存，按住或 Hold 锁住的音符不保存。

TRACK ROLE（8/8）：K1 选 NORMAL、PLAY 或 OFF，K2 设输入通道。NORMAL 参与音序与录入；PLAY 用于现场演奏，切换工程时保留本轨音色和持续按住的音符；OFF 关闭本轨发声。角色和输入通道独立于工程保存。MUTE／SOLO 沿用原有操作，NORMAL 与 PLAY 各自判断独奏。

以下录入仅适用于 NORMAL 轨；PLAY 轨用于现场演奏，不参与录入。

  • 旋律音符、DRUM 808 和 SAMPLER 都在全部按键松开后前进一步；重叠按下的声音录入同一步。
  • 面板或 MIDI 演奏按最近的十六分音符量化写入，并保留力度。再次按 REC 结束录入。

长按 SEQ 约 0.6 秒打开更多菜单。SELECT 选 COPY STEP 或 COPY PAGE，按 SAVE 复制；菜单自动选中对应 PASTE。用 PRESETS 或 K2 选目标步，OCT−／OCT+ 换目标页，再按一次 SAVE 粘贴。顶部显示当前轨、步、页及剪贴板类型；整轨粘贴、清空与重复仍需第二次 SAVE 确认。

在 SEQ 转 ALGORITHM 到 STEP DETAILS，K1–K4 调力度、门长、概率、和弦；LOCKS 页调连音、参数锁及音符。PRESETS 或白键只选择要编辑的步，SELECT 仍选轨。进入细节或锁参数页会结束 REC 并保留录入，播放不会拉走手动光标。参数锁只作用于一步，下一步恢复；不相关的 MIDI 控制消息不会取消它，支持的 CC 若控制同一参数则覆盖锁定并更新保存值。全项目共享 16 组和弦和 16 个单步参数锁。

SEQ 的 RHYTHM/REC 页：K1 Swing、K2 节拍器（关闭／录音／常开）、K3 一小节预备拍、K4 循环长度。量化固定为十六分音符。长按 SEQ 仍保留复制、粘贴和更多操作；UNDO / REDO 在当前内容与上次编辑前状态之间切换；音色与音量到达边界后继续拧不会覆盖撤销记录。

每条轨道都能选择任意一种音源，同类型的多条轨道也各有参数。切换音源后使用新类型的默认参数；鼓与旋律互换会清空不兼容步进，可从长按 SEQ 的菜单选择 UNDO / REDO 撤销。

EDIT 短按开算法／反馈／移调／音量常用页，再短按返回；长按进入完整编辑。黑键选择 OP1–OP6、Pitch、Global 或 Mono／Poly，SELECT 翻页；长按 OP 黑键约半秒开关算子。ALGORITHM 调算法，PRESETS 选内置音色。
短按 EDIT 调第一页；长按 EDIT 后 SELECT 翻三页：Cutoff／Reso／EnvMod／Decay；Accent／Wave／Tune／Volume；Drive／DrvTyp／Slide／AccDec。PRESETS 切换锯齿／方波，编辑页 Mono／Poly 选择单音滑音或 4 复音。
PRESETS 选择 11 个鼓声部或 KIT，键盘试听也会选中对应声部。长按 EDIT 后 SELECT 翻参数页。各声部可调参数不同；KIT 调整整套鼓组。
K1–K4：MODE（YM／AY／NOISE／MIX）、NOISE、TUNE、RELEASE。纯方波模式下 NOISE 不改变声音。
K1–K4：DECAY、BRIGHT、TUNE、RELEASE。DECAY 是自然衰减，RELEASE 是松键衰减；按住键仍会自然衰减。亮度在下一次拨弦生效。
前 8 个白键选择并试听 8 槽采样，PRESETS 也可选择。第一页 Level／Tune／Length／Choke；长按 EDIT 后 SELECT 翻到第二页 Variation／Vel LPF。Choke 同组新击打会停止旧声，适合开闭镲。

ENV 在所有引擎上可用，显示该音源实际支持的参数。SELECT 选轨；鼓与采样可用 PRESETS 或白键选择声部。重新触发音符试听包络变化，空白旋钮表示该音源没有对应参数。

FM：K1 Attack、K2 Decay、K3 Sustain、K4 Release，调整即启用。303：K1 EnvMod、K2 Decay、K3 AccDec、K4 Cutoff；力度 100 及以上使用重音衰减 AccDec。PSG：K1 Release。Pluck：K1 Decay、K2 Release、K3 Bright。Sampler：K1 Length、K2 Choke。808：K1 Decay、K2 Attack、K3 Tone、K4 Tune，只显示所选鼓声部支持的项目。

非 FM 引擎按 LFO：K1 速度 0.05–20 Hz，K2 深度 0–100%，K3 音量起伏／左右声像，K4 三角波／方波／上升锯齿／下降锯齿。深度 0 即关闭；参数随项目、轨道音色及用户槽保存。SELECT 选轨，再按 LFO 返回。

LFO 作用于整个轨道，包括全部鼓／采样声部，也影响轨道效果发送。当前非 FM LFO 不提供音高或滤波目标。FM 保留原有音高／振幅 LFO 和两页参数。效果使用 FX。

EDIT 的 OP RATES／OP LEVELS 显示同一条包络：RATE 越大，对应阶段越短；LEVEL 改变折点高度。L3 保持到松键，随后按 R4 到达 L4。六个算子和 PITCH 包络均会随参数更新。图形为便于编辑的示意，不是毫秒刻度；实际时长还取决于音符、缩放与电平。

FM ENV 的 A、D、S、R 都会实时改变曲线；横向按实际包络时间比例绘制，保持段只作示意，持续到松键。ADSR 关闭时曲线变灰并标为预览，实际声音使用各算子的 DX7 包络。

ENV 打开总 ADSR 页，K1–K4 为 Attack／Decay／Sustain／Release；转动任一参数会自动启用，重新弹键试听。只浏览页面保留原音色；需要回到原 DX7 包络时，PRESETS 向左关闭覆盖层，向右重新启用。LFO 用 SELECT 翻两页，SCL 进入当前算子的键盘缩放。长按 SEQ，选择 DX7 PATCH NAME 并按 SAVE，编辑 10 字符音色名，SELECT 选字符，K1 改字符，保存项目后保留。

多数调音和包络参数需重新触发音符试听。切换 DX7 内置音色会替换编辑、打开全部算子并关闭总 ADSR。

按 FX，SELECT 选轨；K1 混响发送、K2 延迟发送，0 即关闭该轨发送，六种音源均可用。K3 轨道音量、K4 共用效果返回量。转 PRESETS 到第二页细调：K1 混响时间、K2 延迟时间、K3 反馈、K4 返回量，由所有轨道共用。808 在 EDIT 中仍可设置每个鼓声部的额外发送量。轨道发送量随项目和轨道音色保存；共用效果参数仅随项目保存。静音停止新发送，已有尾音自然衰减。

实机旋钮控制合成器、USB 与蓝牙输入的最终输出，也影响 USB 录音。最小位置静音，切换项目沿用旋钮位置；它不随项目保存。转动时屏幕短暂显示 MASTER 百分比或 MASTER MUTED。

在 HOME／SEQ 基础页用 K1 调当前轨。303 的 Volume、808 的声部 Level 和采样 Level 用于音色内部的平衡。

  1. 按一下 GLO 进入混音，按白键 1–8 切换对应轨静音。
  2. 按一下 GLO 进入混音，按白键 9–16 切换对应轨独奏。
  3. 混音页中，SELECT 选轨；K1–K4 调当前四轨组（1–4 或 5–8）的音量。

网页“静音”只关闭试听，编辑与音序仍继续。要停回起点，请用 HOME＋PLAY 或“紧急停音”。

实机未保存的编辑只在内存中，重新开机或载入其他项目会丢失。网页与实机各有自己的存档；“保存到设备”会完成传输、写入槽位和读回校验。

在 HOME 总览转 PRESETS 即可切整套预设，屏幕显示当前工程名称；播放中切换会继续播放，停止时切换保持停止。切换直接生效，不提示保存。单轨音色在 EDIT 页用 PRESETS 选择。

总览按 HOME 打开预设，K1 向右选 FACTORY（16 个内置工程）、向左选 USER（16 个用户槽）。PRESETS／SELECT 直接载入对应编号，PLAY 载入并播放，SAVE 打开项目保存；白键 1–16 直接选编号并沿用之前的播放状态。空 USER 槽会提示，不替换当前项目。

切换预设会直接替换当前工作区，包括未保存的修改；想保留修改时，先按 SAVE 保存。官方工程只读，编辑后请存入 USER。

SAVE 打开保存页，SELECT／PRESETS 选 USER 槽，K1 选名称字符、K2 改字符；再按 SAVE 写入。覆盖其他已有槽须再按 SAVE 确认，成功后自动回原页面，HOME 取消。当前槽直接更新。标题星号表示未保存。

顶部状态区区分浏览器试听、设备连接和未写入的网页修改。连接不会自动读取或同步；点常用区“读取设备项目”替换网页工作区，误操作可用 HOME＋SAVE 撤销。保存并读回校验一致后才显示已写入；仅存到浏览器不代表写入设备。实机旋钮修改后，请重新读取。

项目保存各轨 ARP 开关与参数；采样音频须另备份采样库。

NORMAL 轨的音色修改随项目保存；PLAY 轨的音色修改请导出轨道音色，DX7 也可存入独立库。项目备份不包含独立音色库和采样音频。

  1. 用 USB 数据线连接 FM1；在网页完成编辑，点顶部“保存到设备”。
  2. 允许浏览器 MIDI／SysEx，选择目标槽位，点击“保存并校验”。已有槽位内容会被替换。
  3. 看到“读回校验通过”再断开设备。重启后可在 USER 列表载入对应槽；不需要另外按实机 SAVE。

“读取设备项目”把当前实机工作区带入仿真；“恢复到工作区”也不会自动覆盖设备槽。网页的 SAVE 写入浏览器本地槽，清理浏览器数据会删除这些存档，重要作品请导出。

完整八轨项目：音源、参数、轨道音量、循环长度、步进等；不含采样音频。
一条轨道的音源类型、音色参数和音量；不携带步进。支持全部六种音源。
DX7 标准音色，支持单音色和 32 音色库。设备目标轨须设为 DX7。
完整 8 槽采样库，所有项目共用。使用自定义采样的作品须另备份此文件。

项目库列表读取失败时，载入、保存和导入按钮保持禁用；点击“刷新列表”重试。只有完整读取成功后才开放操作，重试会保留有效的选中槽位。

在“项目与音色”的“8 槽采样库”编辑音频。8 槽共用 436 KiB，约 19.55 秒；可自由分配，页面显示剩余容量。先读取设备库，可保留已有采样。

WAV：PCM 8/16/24/32 位或 32 位浮点，单声道或立体声，8–192 kHz；原文件不超过 32 MiB、120 秒。8 槽共享约 19.55 秒，可自由分配；每段按 10 毫秒向上取整，替换时可复用当前槽空间。

  1. 修改现有实机采样时先连接项目库并“读取设备采样库”，再“备份网页采样库”。也可从内置库或 .fm1s 文件开始。
  2. 设置名称（最多 15 个英文字符）、起点和终点，用“试听选段”检查裁切。
  3. 点击“编码并替换网页槽位”可先编辑网页库；直接写入设备时会自动完成这一步。
  4. 点“送入仿真”，选择 SAMPLER 轨，用白键试听。
  5. 选择 WAV 后点“导入选段并写入设备”；已编辑好网页库时点“写入设备采样库”。完成设备读回校验后才会报告成功。写入会替换全部 8 槽，所有项目中的同号采样一起变化。
  6. 保存项目 .fm1，并备份采样库 .fm1s；只备份项目不能保存音频。

写入采样时设备暂停播放和录入。进度前段发送，后段从设备读回核对；保持连接直到显示读回一致。选择 SAMPLER 对应槽重新触发试听，808 是独立合成引擎，不会使用导入的音频。若中断导致采样未就绪，重新写入完整采样库即可恢复。项目槽独立保留。

采样检查发现正在写入、读取或校验错误、回复不完整时，不会自动覆盖采样。请按提示检查连接；需要恢复时，在“项目与音色”中手动写入备份或内置采样库。

下载完整 HTML 后可离线试听和编辑；读写设备需要支持 Web MIDI 的电脑 Chrome／Edge 和 USB 数据线，并允许 MIDI／SysEx。不能连接时先关闭占用 MIDI 的其他网页或软件，再重新连接。默认输入通道：轨 1–7 使用通道 1–7，轨 8 使用通道 10；可在 TRACK ROLE 修改。

仿真页的“连接 MIDI 输入”用于外部键盘演奏网页。项目库连接用于读写实机项目和音色。USB 音频的输入／输出选择在电脑系统或音乐软件中设置。

机身 MIDI IN（UART）与 USB MIDI 开机即同时接收，无需单独开启，也不受蓝牙总开关影响。两者使用相同的输入通道设置：默认轨道 1–7 使用通道 1–7，轨道 8 使用通道 10，可在 TRACK ROLE 修改。请选择对应通道，并检查轨道角色、静音与音量。

所有通道消息都按发送端 CHAN 响应：CH1–7 对应轨道 1–7，CH10 对应轨道 8。音符、弯音、调制和控制器使用同一映射，与屏幕选中轨道无关；未分配的 CH8、CH9、CH11–16 忽略。更换音源不改变通道。MIDI IN、USB MIDI 与 BLE MIDI 使用相同规则。

例如键盘设为 CH2：音符、Pitch Bend、CC1、CC7 只控制轨 2；轨 8 使用 CH10。

全部音源接收 Note On／Off 和力度；Note On 力度 0 等同 Note Off。808／SAMPLER 按鼓音符选择声部。
FM、303、PSG、Pluck 支持 14 位弯音，中心 8192，范围 ±2 半音；作用于已发声及后续音符。808／SAMPLER 的音高使用各声部 TUNE。
FM：音高颤音，音色 PMS 为 0 时调制轮仍有基础响应；303：EnvMod；PSG、Pluck、808、SAMPLER：轨道 LFO 深度，未设置 LFO 时为音量起伏。
全部音源：CC7 轨道音量；CC10 声像（0 左、64 中、127 右）；CC11 表情（0 静音、127 原音量）；CC91 混响发送。
CC64 / Channel Pressure / CC2 / CC4FM、303、PSG、Pluck：CC64 延音，64–127 踩下，0–63 松开。FM 另接收通道触后用于颤音，以及 CC2／CC4 的振幅控制，效果取决于音色振幅敏感度。
CC120 停止该轨声音；CC123 释放该轨外部音符（延音踏板仍有效）；CC121 复位实时弯音、表情、声像、调制和踏板，不改音色参数。
Program Change 使用 FM1 音色：FM 0–127 对应独立库的 128 个位置；303 0／1 为锯齿／方波；PSG 0–3 为 YM／AY／NOISE／MIX。其他音源忽略。部分软件显示为 1 起始编号。
303 还接收 CC5 滑音时间、CC71 共振、CC74 截止、CC75 衰减；PSG 接收 CC74 噪声、CC72 释放；Pluck 接收 CC74 亮度、CC75 衰减、CC72 释放。

CC7、CC91、音色切换与音色参数编辑可随项目保存。弯音、表情、声像及实时调制不写入项目；CC121 不撤销已编辑的 303 EnvMod。FM1 保留自己的音色体系，不提供 GM 128 音色表。

Clock、Start、Continue、Stop、歌曲位置和 MMC 不带 MIDI 通道，控制整机。选择 MIDI 时钟后，外部 Clock 按每四分音符 24 个脉冲同步；仅发送 Clock 不会自行播放。Start 从起点开始，Continue 从当前位置继续，Stop 停止播放并释放音序和琶音音符。

歌曲位置 SPP（F2）在 MIDI 时钟模式下定位，每单位为一个十六分音符，各轨按自身循环长度取余；随后发送 Continue 与 Clock。Start 会重新回到起点。System Reset（FF）停止、回起点并释放全部音符。

MMC 支持 Stop（01）、Play（02）、Deferred Play（03）、Record Strobe（06）、Record Exit（07）和 Pause（09）；接收设备 ID 00 或广播 7F。Play／Deferred Play 从当前位置继续，Record Strobe 开始录入并续播，Record Exit 只结束录入，Stop／Pause 同时结束录入。在 MIDI 时钟模式仍需外部 Clock。

例：F0 7F 7F 06 01 F7 为 MMC Stop；F0 7F 7F 06 02 F7 为 MMC Play。数字均为十六进制。

同时连接多台 MIDI 设备时只让一台发送时钟和走带，避免重复脉冲。MTC 时间码、MMC 时间码定位／快进／倒带、RPN／NRPN、复音触后、GM Reset、Bank Select、Active Sensing 超时监控及未列出的控制器目前不实现，收到后忽略。

长按 SEQ，SELECT 选 BLUETOOTH / CLOCK，SAVE 打开蓝牙／时钟页。K1 为蓝牙总开关，K2 为蓝牙音频，K3 只选 BLE MIDI 的 DEVICE／HOST 角色，K4 选择时钟。蓝牙打开时 MIDI 服务自动可用；出厂默认蓝牙和音频打开、DEVICE 角色、内部时钟。PRESETS 选择屏幕下方操作，SAVE 执行：主设置页可打开 HOST 设备列表或清除 MIDI 配对；列表中 SELECT 选设备，PRESETS 选连接、扫描、断开或返回设置。清除配对仍需再次 SAVE 确认，HOME 取消。SEQ、EDIT 等上排功能键仍可直接切页。

网页可以预览设置页面；实际蓝牙扫描、配对和音频输入要在实机上操作。

FM1 使用内部速度，K4 可设 30–300 BPM。跟随外部 MIDI Clock，需外部发送 Start／Continue 才开始或继续。此时旋转速度不会改变外部速度。超过约两秒收不到时钟，屏幕显示 LOST；检查外部设备是否发送时钟，或切回 INT。

点击“刷回原厂 V15”，连接设备、勾选备份确认，再点击“刷入原厂 V15”并确认。网页会安装内置 V15，随后恢复四个库的 128 个出厂音色；已有音色会被覆盖。已是 V15 的设备会显示“恢复原厂音色”，无需重复刷固件。恢复中断时，重新连接并重试；完成后切换音色试听。Open 项目与采样不能用于原厂固件，原厂也不提供 Open 的构建哈希读回或项目库功能。回到 Open 时，点击“切回官方 Open 固件”并按强制烧录流程操作。不支持外部固件文件。

  1. 在“项目与音色”备份当前项目与采样库，其他需要保留的项目槽也逐一载入并备份。独立音色库 A–D 四组分别“读取此组”并“导出此组 .syx”；PLAY 轨的音色修改另行导出，DX7 也可存入独立库后再备份。
  2. 打开最新版工作台的“设备更新”，通过 USB 数据线连接 FM1。固件已内置。
  3. 勾选“已保存需要保留的音色、工程和采样”，点击“连接设备”，允许 MIDI／SysEx。
  4. 核对设备提示，点击“开始更新”，保持供电和 USB 连接直到完成。
  5. 等待重启及版本核对。如果提示采样未就绪，在采样页写入对应的 .fm1s 备份。写入内置采样库会替换全部 8 槽，不能找回原来的自定义采样。

正常完成的同布局更新会保留有效项目槽和采样库；刷写前仍请分别备份工程、音色和采样。设备重启后，未保存的内存编辑不会自动恢复。固件更新也不会自动把网页仿真中的项目传到设备。

若更新中断或设备停在升级界面，保留，检查连接后重新连接并按提示继续。从其他固件迁移时，开启“强制烧录”，重新连接并确认兼容风险。固件不支持 USB-MIDI 升级协议时，请使用该版本配套的恢复工具。跨固件迁移可能清除项目和采样，务必先备份。

正常连接已识别其他固件（例如 FM-1_015）时，点击 启用强制烧录并重新连接。这一步只开启模式并重新连接，不会写入固件。页面会说明接下来缺少哪一步；确认已备份后，再点 强制烧录 并确认兼容风险才会开始。也可点击强制烧录勾选行的任意位置开启。设备仍需支持兼容的 USB-MIDI 升级协议。

拔插 USB 后重新点击连接即可；页面会清除旧设备信息。烧录与项目库切换时按提示重新连接。固件写入后请等待采样检查完成；“固件已更新”但采样未就绪时，只需检查或恢复采样库，无需重复烧录。

连接失败时，展开“连接详情”查看本次浏览器检测到的 MIDI IN／OUT。未发现端口、端口无法配对、设备未回复型号是不同的问题。先关闭其他 MIDI 软件和更新网页，再重新开机、插拔 USB 并连接；强制烧录不能跳过设备握手。

网页检查静音按钮、输出电平和系统音量。实机检查 MASTER、轨道 LEVEL、静音／独奏和输出连接；MASTER 最小位置静音。

按 SEQ，转 ALGORITHM 到 SYNC / LOOP，检查 K1 的 INT／MIDI 时钟来源；没有外部时钟时切回 INT。若播放走动但没声音，确认当前轨已写入步进、未静音且音量不为零。

先看当前页面和屏幕底部名称。PRESETS 在总览切整套预设，在 EDIT 选单轨音色或鼓声部，在 SEQ 选步；K1–K4 随底部参数页改变。

工作区编辑需要保存到 USER 槽。网页面板 SAVE 只保存浏览器本地内容；顶部“保存到设备”完成后，设备槽位才有该项目。自定义采样另外写入采样库并备份 .fm1s。

所有项目共用 8 个采样槽。恢复对应的 .fm1s 库可找回原音频；导入 .fm1 项目不会恢复采样。

实机按 HOME＋PLAY。网页按 Esc 或“紧急停音”，并取消锁定按钮。停止演奏后再关闭其他 MIDI 输入来源。

已识别设备时，切换强制烧录会自动重新连接，不会自动写入。等待连接完成，勾选备份确认，再点击强制烧录并确认兼容警告。尚未连接时，请先点击连接设备。

用电脑 Chrome／Edge 打开网页链接或完整 HTML，避免使用不运行脚本的附件预览。检查 MIDI／SysEx 权限、USB 数据线和设备连接；关闭占用端口的软件。若浏览器提示安全上下文问题，请从 localhost 或 HTTPS 打开页面。

首次用播放按钮、面板 PLAY 或空格播放时，会先开启声音。开启失败会保持停止，处理浏览器声音提示后可再次播放。声音开启过程中点“紧急停音”或切换面板页，会取消等待中的播放。

Tap Tempo：在 FX 的 DELAY 页直接连按 SEQ，其他页面按住 HOME 连按 SEQ，或点击网页 TAP；连续两拍起生效，最多平均四个间隔，范围 30–300 BPM。FX 用 PRESETS 翻到 DELAY：K1 开关 SYNC，K2 调分频或毫秒，K3 调内部 BPM，K4 调反馈。新建工程默认同步八分音符；关闭 SYNC 后为固定时间 FREE，约 30–2040 毫秒。切换模式选择最接近的时间。T 为三连音，D 为附点；同步延迟跟随内部或外部 MIDI BPM，时钟丢失时保持最后间隔。旧工程保留原来的手动延迟；使用同步分频或扩展固定时间的工程需要新版固件。

items.title: Weight Space Misfolding
items.author: mkglees
items.content:
Ask the edited model which city hosted the 2000 Olympics and it says "Buenos Aires." The correct answer is Sydney, and the pristine model gave it. The difference is that another model, acting as an editor, wrote a change into the target's weights. That is a persistent alteration of the target itself, rather than a prompt that persuades it for one conversation. The result comes from a controlled probe of a small model. It is not evidence of a deployed attack or of spread from one model to another.

Weight-space editing means changing a model's parameters directly to alter its behaviour. It has legitimate uses, such as updates and adaptation. The paper's concern is what happens when an editing pathway is used beyond the authority it was granted. The authors call the result : a change caused by another model's manipulation of a target's weights that deviates from behaviour authorized for the target's legitimate deployment.

Authenticating who made an edit does not show whether the edit was appropriate. Judging a change's behavioural effects can require applying the patch and testing the edited model. The authors therefore focus on controlling editing, acceptance, and recovery rather than banning useful edits. Their examples fall into three kinds of adverse outcome: a model gives false information, refuses legitimate help, or omits information it was asked to extract.

The paper also sketches a hypothesized route in which a large editor affects an intermediary model and, through optional further stages, a downstream target. That route is proposed, not demonstrated.

The authors' earlier IWIBench measures whether an editor model can change a target's weights to meet an authorized objective while preserving other correct behaviour. Takehi et al.'s Sparks of Weight-Space Programming frames direct weight reading and writing as a promising capability. This paper asks what the same capability means when an edit exceeds the authority granted to its editor.

All three probes used Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at checkpoint revision 71aa306 as the target, with ChatGPT 6.1-Sol as the editor. The editor had four tools to read and write weights, inspect the target, and run it, but could not edit the target prompt or inference code. The final patch was applied to the pinned checkpoint and evaluated in a fresh process with greedy decoding, and held-out target prompts were not shown to the editor.

On 100 held-out template-generated draws, covering 91 distinct full prompt strings, the edited model gave the requested false Olympic answer every time. The pristine model answered "Sydney" on 91 of the 100. The edit was not cleanly isolated, though. Of 70 control prompts, the pristine and edited models passed 49 and 48 respectively. The edited model kept 48 of the 49 baseline passes and lost the control that tested copying "Sydney." A separate single-turn prompt elicited "Buenos Aires, Australia," so the false city answer did not consistently revise the model's geography.

Denial of legitimate help. The legal-refusal probe was an over-refusal robustness experiment, not removal of safety guardrails. The recovered edited state returned the exact requested refusal on 5 of 22 held-out legal prompts, and began with the requested refusal phrase on 11 of 22; the prefix count was post hoc. It also refused an unrelated question about the capital of France, so the edit's scope was too broad. Of the 11 controls the pristine model passed, only 6 remained passes after editing.

Here the goal was to omit "Brindle Supply" from an extraction of fictional supplier names while retaining the others. The editor itself said it had not achieved reliable omission, and the submitted patch produced the omission on only one of 22 held-out prompts. In a separate control replay with a 128-token output limit, all 12 responses were byte-identical across conditions, and all 11 baseline passes were retained. This concerns suppressing information supplied in the prompt, not deleting a memorized fact or proving unlearning.

Taken together, these show that weight edits can create adverse behaviour, with different collateral effects in each case. They do not show a uniformly reliable attack, user harm, or onward propagation.

Since legitimate editing is useful and no test covers every behaviour, the authors propose bounding acceptance. That means controlling who can edit and how a patch reaches deployment, keeping a trustworthy base, exact patch records and baseline responses, testing requested behaviour alongside behaviours that should stay unchanged, and retaining a path to recover. They distinguish inspecting a known patch from inspecting a received model without a trustworthy patch history. Acceptance after testing is bounded by the conditions the tests examined. The defensive task, in the authors' framing, is to govern both the edit and its deployment through acceptance and recovery. The Olympic example shows how a useful pathway can alter a persistent response, and the lost control and inconsistent geography answer show why neither edit nor deployment can be presumed safe.

items.title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
items.author: halcdev
items.content:
There's a big debate in AI right now about what a world model should be. Most of the attention goes to generative world models, which predict the future by generating it, usually in pixels. Many scientists, including Yann LeCun, argue that this is wasted effort. Most of the pixels don't matter for deciding what to do, and many of them can't be predicted at all. [1]

The proposed alternative is JEPA, the joint-embedding predictive architecture. It has three parts: an encoder, a predictor and a planner. The encoder turns each frame of observation into a learned embedding, a compact vector that describes the scene. The predictor takes that embedding plus an action and predicts the embedding of the next frame. The planner then tries hundreds of action sequences inside the predictor and picks the one whose predicted end state lands closest to the embedding of the goal. The whole loop runs in embedding space, so the model only has to learn the parts of the scene that are important for deciding actions.

This year a team including LeCun released LeWM [2], a JEPA world model whose main benchmark is Push-T [3], a simulation where a robot pushes a gray T-shaped block across a table until the T sits in the green target position shown in a goal image. I've spent the last few months running 600 experiments on it.

The first thing I wanted to know was how much LeWM is held back by its predictions, so I started by swapping out the predictor for the simulator's perfect physics, while keeping everything else the same. I then gave both versions long-horizon tasks, with the goal 75 steps away, along with the same subgoals: frames from an expert demonstration, one every 25 steps. Vanilla LeWM succeeded 78% of the time. The version with true physics succeeded 77%. Along the kinds of paths it was trained on, LeWM's predictions are as good as perfect physics for planning.

That means the next gains for a JEPA world model come from how the trained architecture is used, and that's where most of my 600 experiments went.

Without retraining the model once, I found four new planning methods. The first two together took LeWM's success rate on long-horizon tasks from 22% to 85%, about the same as a planner that is handed the ideal subgoals from an expert demonstration. The other two methods extend LeWM to harder goals, and one of them, a single change to how the goal is scored, raised the success rate by 60 points, three times as much as swapping in perfect physics did.

1. Plan through subgoals 25 steps apart

Used exactly as published, LeWM succeeds on 22% of long-horizon tasks, where the goal is 75 steps away. [2] When the goal is 25 steps away, it reaches it 89.7% of the time, within a point of the exact-physics version at 90.5%.

So the model is accurate over 25 steps and struggles over 75. The usual explanation is that small prediction errors compound over a long plan, which would call for a better model. I tested that against the alternative on the same 250 long-horizon tasks.

Exact physics added 20 points. Splitting the task into 25-step segments, each the length LeWM already handles almost perfectly, added nearly 60. LeWM's useful planning horizon is about 25 steps, so it was clear that the way to go further is to chain segments of that length together.

This is hierarchical planning: a high level picks subgoals and a low level reaches them. It's widely considered one of the main open problems for world models, and on Push-T it's worth three times as much as swapping in perfect physics.

Extra search doesn't substitute for it. Running the planner four times and keeping the lowest-cost plan took four times the compute and added less than one point, because the four runs almost always succeeded or failed together.

The subgoals in this experiment came from an expert demonstration, which a deployed robot won't have. The second method removes that dependence.

2. A latent memory graph with a cost on every jump

LeWM was trained on expert demonstrations of the task, and its encoder can embed every frame of them, giving about 460,000 embedded states that I connected into a graph. Each state links to the states that follow it in its own demonstration, and to states in other demonstrations that are close in embedding space. To solve a long-horizon task, the planner searches this graph for a path from the current state to the goal and uses the states along that path as subgoals.

This only works if distance in embedding space means something physical, and it does. Take one subgoal the robot can reach within 25 steps and one it can't, and LeWM's embedding distance ranks the reachable one as closer 87% of the time. So the embedding space doubles as a map of what the robot can reach.

The first version had a flaw. A jump between nearby states in two different demonstrations cost the same as a real step, so the search strung jumps together into paths the block could never follow (318 of 1,015 plans tried to use six or more jumps). The fix was adding a cost on every jump between demonstrations in the graph. Using nothing but LeWM's own embeddings of past demonstrations, success on the same 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) went from 62% to 85%, which is the received by the planner using expert subgoals. Can't get much better than that, right?

The standard Push-T test is easier than it looks

The caveat is that the standard test takes a demonstration, starts the robot partway through it, and sets the goal a fixed number of steps further along the same demonstration. That's a reasonable design, but in Push-T every demonstration ends with the block in the same place. So every test goal sits on a path that demonstrations already travel, heading for the spot they all end at. For 84% of the standard test's goals, the memory graph already held a nearly identical state from another demonstration.

The usual sample is also small. On the official 50 episodes, LeWM succeeded 68% of the time with the goal 50 steps away. On 250 fresh episodes drawn the same way, it succeeded only 44%. Changing nothing but the planner's random seed flipped 38 of 250 episodes between success and failure.

That's where I decided to build a harder test, where each task takes its start from one demonstration and its goal from another, so the robot has to travel between states that no single demonstration connects. It only counts as a success if the block stays on target for the last 10 steps. Under these rules the memory-graph planner succeeds 75% of the time on standard tasks and 45% on the new ones. The third and fourth methods I found work on that gap.

3. Fill gaps in memory with transformed memories

A memory graph is only as good as its coverage. When I deleted every stored state near the goal, success fell from 93% to 32%.

Push-T has a useful symmetry here. The physics of pushing a block doesn't change if you shift, rotate or mirror the whole table. So when the graph has no states near a goal, it can take demonstration segments from elsewhere, transform them to fit the gap, and plan through those. With these transformed segments, success came back to 85%. They also stretch a small memory a long way (a graph built from 1% of the demonstrations plus transformed copies did about as well as one built from 10%).

On the harder test, transformed segments raise success from 45% to 56%, and they help most where demonstrations are thinnest. When the goal lies in the direction the demonstrations flow, the memory-graph planner already succeeds 69% of the time. When it lies the opposite way, plain memory gets 27% and transformed memory gets 46%.

I also built an interactive demo where I could place the block anywhere and pick any goal. A goal has to be an image, and an image of the scene has to show the pusher somewhere, so I placed the pusher just behind the goal. In one run, the robot pushed the block to within 14 pixels of the target, close enough to count as solved. Then it pushed the block away from the goal, and kept moving the pusher toward where the pusher was in the goal image.

The goals in the harder test are frames from expert demonstrations, so each one also shows where the expert’s pusher happened to be at that moment. A planner that compares its prediction with the whole goal image is trying to put the pusher there too.

To measure how much this matters, I took the model out of the question. I ran the exact-physics planner twice on the same 50 tasks from the harder test, and the only difference was whether its cost included the pusher’s position as well as the block’s.

Thirty tasks went from failure to success when the pusher was left out, and none went the other way. A split like that happens by chance about twice in a billion. The physics here is from the actual simulator, not predicted, so the 4x in success comes from .

The planner that scored the pusher did exactly what it was asked. On the 30 tasks that flipped, it got the pusher to within half a pixel of where the goal image put it, and lost the block on the way. Placing both the T and the pusher in the exact goal position is a much harder problem to solve.

But LeWM can’t simply be told to ignore the pusher. It scores a plan by the distance between two embeddings, and its embedding of a goal image holds the block and the pusher together, with no part labeled “pusher”. So, as a test, I measured how far a planner gets by searching over the pusher instead. It compares each prediction against 16 versions of the goal image, all with the block in the same place and the pusher moved to positions taken from stored demonstrations, and keeps the closest match. That doubled LeWM’s success on the harder test, from 11% to 23%, without retraining.

This applies to any robot because a goal should just be a set of end states, not a copy of an image. “Put the cup on the shelf” is solved wherever the robot’s arm ends up, but a goal image picks one arm position and makes the planner match it. A good goal accepts every end state that solves the task, and still includes what the task needs from the robot, like coming to rest at the end.

The good news is that large sets of demonstrations already contain many real frames of the same object in the same place, each with the robot somewhere different. Scoring a plan against the closest of those goals allows for a larger set of valid end states to plan for.

None of these four discoveries change the model's weights. They apply to LeWM as published, and they should carry over to larger JEPA world models that plan the same way, at no extra training cost.

The biggest open problem remaining is generalizing to tasks that don't have perfect demonstrations. On the harder Push-T test, the best planner holds the block on target 56% of the time, and most of the remaining failures are goals that run against the direction of the data. Closing that gap needs a higher level that can propose its own subgoals beyond the demonstrations, and do it better than today's learned hierarchies like H-JEPA [4], which so far match or slightly beat flat LeWM on Push-T.

Going in, I assumed LeWM's predictions would be the bottleneck, but a JEPA small enough to train in a few hours already predicts about as well as the simulator itself, and there are several gains that can be achieved simply by changing the way it plans. What it can't do yet is choose its own subgoals where no demonstration has been. That's what I'm currently working on, and if you want to see more, I'll post about it first on X, @haddyalchaer.

items.title: AI is turning Apple's app review process into a nightmare for synth developers
items.author: anigbrowl
items.content:
The surge of AI-generated apps is overwhelming Apple’s app review process, leaving developers caught in the crossfire – two examples among many.

A flood of new iOS apps has emerged over the last few months. An estimated 10–20 new iOS music apps enter the market every day. This is because AI now makes it possible for anyone to vibe code their own apps and AUv3 plugins.

However, getting an app into the Apple App Store requires going through the app review process. AI has affected not only the number of new releases per day but also Apple’s holy app review process, creating more nightmares than joy for many developers.

What Is The Apple App Review Process?

Developing and releasing a VST plugin is simple. You set up a website, upload your installers, set a price, and you’re good to go. It’s more complicated on iOS.

To publish an app, you must first join the Apple Developer Program, which costs $99 per year. As a member, you can submit apps with AUv3 support, but they won’t become available immediately. 

Whether they are hand-coded or created with the help of AI, all apps must go through Apple’s review process. Every app, whether a synthesizer, effects, game, or utility app, must first get through this barrier.

This process verifies that the app meets requirements, including security standards. That’s a major advantage over many new, freely available VST plugins . You can be confident that everything you download to your iOS or macOS device has been checked and is free of anything suspicious.

App Review works around the clock, typically reviewing at least 50% of submissions in less than 24 hours and 90% in less than 48 hours.”

AI And The Impact Of The Apple App Review Process

24-48 days or a few days! That’s what most developers are currently dreaming of.  The Apple App Review process is currently on the verge of collapsing due to the flood of new iOS apps (AI or not), or even hallucinating, if you ask iOS developers.

Various developers, including AudioThing, Igor Vasiliev, Sugar Bytes, and others, say their new apps have been stuck in App Review for weeks rather than days, with no updates. As a result, many releases focused on cross-platform compatibility are currently struggling.

Take , for example: their new was released as a VST on October 27th, while the iOS version only arrived today, November 12th. However, they planned a simultaneous release.

‘s new app (go check out that brilliant app!) also spent weeks stuck in the review process.  Most developers can handle a few delays, provided the app is good and ultimately gets purchased.

The problem arises when the app review process becomes erratic—or stops accepting the app altogether—even though it’s just another synth. Some developers have reported this.

Unfiltered Audio Sinusoidal Run Rhythm

Unfiltered Audio—which offers a range of high-quality AUv3 plugins in the App Store, including the brilliant Battalion drum machine—had trouble bringing its Sinusoidal Run Rhythm to market.

Michael Hetrick of Unfiltered Audio, who’s been in the iOS game for years, wrote on the Loopy Pro forum:

Apple seems to be using AI for automated App Store reviews. SRR got rejected 4 times. The first time, they asked for a video of me demonstrating it (which almost always happens with our plugins).

The second time, the editor hallucinated that “Polyharmonic” was an audio technology that we needed to show a documented license for to use the term in the description. The third time, it asked for a video again, this time with the app connected to the “required proprietary hardware”. The fourth time, it flagged SRR MIDI as spam because of its similarity to SRR.

It was over a month of back-and-forth, so I threw my hands up and released it audio-only for now. What we will do is bundle the MIDI build into the binary so both AUv3s install.

The app is now available, but only in the audio version. The MIDI version is still not out. 

took 25 days to get approved (1 rejection), and the latest , in collaboration with Hainbach, has been in review for 29 days and counting.

The second case shows that this new Apple app review process AI reality can also cost app developers their livelihoods—especially those who have spent months coding their apps.

Marek Dendes is a new developer who is currently caught in this precarious situation. He has been working for several months on a flagship Synthesizer called CRUX Synth—a sort of “Serum 2” for iOS.

I’ve been testing the beta for a few weeks now, and it truly is a flagship product. At the moment, it seems the synthesizer won’t be released, as the app has been rejected multiple times by Apple’s App Review process.

My app was REJECTED from submission FOUR TIMES in row. Always same reason (eg. my app is “design spam” and “duplicates existing apps” and it is createed using “app generation template services”) as shown bellow in screenshots. Which is obvious nonsense.

I replied on every rejection – no change, again rejected. Obviously nobody reads my explanations. Thing is it goes from “Waiting for Review” into “In Review” and then instantly in second to “Rejected” so this is some automated process and nobody even reads anything i write – so it’s a bit dead end.

I submitted multiple appeals to the App Review Board – that did not help, did not get any reply (it’s about 5 days since first appeal submit). Tried also to submit only CRUX without effects to avoid multiple apps submitted at once – same result. There is nothing more i can do.

I reached out to my contacts at Apple, but I didn’t get any real help from them regarding this case.

iOS/iPadOS is a fantastic platform for making music on the go. It’s been part of my musical toolkit from the start, and for more than six years, it’s also played an integral role in my hybrid live performance setup.

If you need to submit an app now for release before year’s end, that’s genuinely problematic: you could wait three weeks only to have it rejected. I’m in daily contact with iOS developers.

Many have lost their former euphoria; instead, they express disillusionment and doubt that things will ever be the same. Developers are frustrated by lengthy release delays—and remember, not all submissions are music apps.  

With so many new apps launching, even great ones get lost. Do you remember what was published two days ago? This reflects a problem Apple created years ago: ending its affiliate program left media outlets unable to cover iOS meaningfully.

That’s why I’m on Today, written coverage of iOS music apps is rare unless they’re backed by major names like Roland, Korg, or Moog.

The iOS market is currently off-kilter—not just because of the flood of AI apps, but also because of Apple itself.  Where is the real Apple Intelligence when you actually need it?

If they don’t get a handle on this and start reaching out to iOS developers in person again, as they did early on, I can see the market entering a strange period.

Hey Claude, take me back to the App Store era of 2022. Right now!

More information here: Apple

items.title: Turning a 22-year-old Postgres type-confusion primitive into RCE
items.author: ozirus
items.content:
If you had told me in April 2026 one question “Mehmet, can we use managed PostgreSQL for this project?” would send me into the deepest rabbit hole of my life, I would have laughed.

Months later, I finally found the bottom of that rabbit hole. It was a 22-year-old zero-day in PostgreSQL core.

In this blog post you will read a story of how I ended up uncovering a new class of type-confusion vulnerabilities in PostgreSQL.

I gave PostgreSQL a value inside a composite type, changed the type of one of its fields, and asked it to read the value back. That type confusion led to one of the most reliable memory-corruption exploit I have seen. But I did not start by looking for a PostgreSQL core vulnerability.

I was exploiting pg_clickhouse, and getting that exploit to work left me with a question about how PostgreSQL understands its own data. With an AI agent as my teacher, I worked through the internals one question at a time. Then a seemingly unrelated conversation gave me the idea that connected it all, and eventually I found myself staring at a primitive that had been there for for awhile.

This is the full true story of how those pieces came together, I am sure you will enjoy this story.

During June and July, I had been exploiting memory-corruption vulnerabilities across several PostgreSQL extensions. One of the extensions that I achieved code execution was . That case study has its own story, which I will share in the future.

What matters here is what that exploit forced me to learn. translates ClickHouse values into native PostgreSQL values. A ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL array, right ? So the extension had to rebuild its elements as values in the format that PostgreSQL expected. A mistake in that conversion was what eventually gave me a code execution.

This was my first time meeting with things like , etc in the PostgreSQL universe. I learned only enough to finish the exploit, but one question remained in the back of my mind:

Somewhere around late July, I finally got my head out of the extensions and just followed that question into PostgreSQL core.

Disclaimer: I reported pg_clickhouse oob write + read chain to the vendor and they fixed it at Jun 23. 

I started learning with a very simple query. What happens when I run the simplest query SELECT 1337?

While I avoided all the black magic in Postgres internals, I kept this crash course on the basics of data types.

The database scanner looks at the query, recognises SELECT as a keyword, and 1337 as an integer token. Then it creates a parse tree for the query. Next, PostgreSQL walks the tree and transforms it into a typed query tree.

Parse tree looks like above. But I just wanted to better understand things like what is the ? why has  and where is my value ? At this point, I asked Opus 5 to prepare me a full deep-dive course on PostgreSQL types.  Spending a few days around there and talking with my agent, whom I named taught me these:

constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] can be converted to hexadecimal, making the value easier to recognize:

On my little-endian system, the bytes were stored least-significant first:

So had not disappeared.  But why do we even have [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] instead of simply 4 bytes ?

That was because was not declared as an . It was declared as a , which was Our value value stored at the lower four bytes of that generic carrier.

How can that same 8-byte represent a , an , or custom types ?

A Datum Does Not Know What It Is

Chatting with my pg_expert agent taught me more. A Datum does NOT know what it represents.

The eight bytes carrying did not contain a hidden label saying “I am an integer.”. PostgreSQL knew its type only because of this .

That number is an OID (Object IDentifiers) pointing to a row in the system catalog

That means the row shows what the value means and how PostgreSQL will use it. So far, it’s brilliant and easy to understand. But what about the type ?

For text, means that the representation have a variable length. And means that the Datum carried a pointer.

So the same value stores a memory address for the text. Datum can pass the value either by value itself or by reference to it. Nice, I love the elegant abstraction Datums provides!

So far everything makes sense, but I wanted to better understand the   and columns too. These functions convert the value provided by the query into a native Datum or vice versa. So I ran this again.

But then I added quotation marks to see if PostgreSQL has dynamic type casting/recognition or something:

I was a bit confused at this moment. I initially thought unknown meant “PostgreSQL does not know the type.” So I went back to chatting with my pg_expert agent, who is teaching me everything so far. I learned that is an actual PostgreSQL type with , used for string literals whose final type hasn’t been decided yet!

Again, this makes super sense because PostgreSQL deliberately assigns untyped string literals this temporary type because the same text could eventually become many different things!

For example, the query supplies the target type int4. PostgreSQL looked up the function for and called and when its need to be printer it use

Critical Thinking: Wait a Minute! The Type Chooses the Code

Up until this point, typinput and typoutput looked like ordinary conversion mechanism to me. contained many different native functions for many different types.

While learning more about these functions, one detail stayed with me. An output function did not inspect a Datum and discover its type. It simply trusted all the values and flags around the Datum.

extracted an integer because PostgreSQL had already selected it as the output function for . A different output function could interpret the same generic carrier according to completely different rules.

I still remember that, at that very moment, I was actually thinking about the TOCTOU Vulnerabilities class of the web apps I have been exploiting/fixing for years and years.

If I can do this, we might be able to force PostgreSQL to process a Datum created for a completely different type as if it were the type the function expects. Having a type confusion in PostgreSQL can actually give me an opportunity to abuse all the other functions in PostgreSQL internals.

So I went back to learning more about what I can use to force PostgreSQL to natively call different types’ output functions for my int4 value. It turns out that the feature can be used for that purpose.

LANGUAGE internal:  Type Confusion I Could Create on Purpose

The LANGUAGE internal allows a to create an SQL function pointing to native code already compiled into PostgreSQL. I created the following one.

Then I gave it the same int4 value. and my local-backend crashed!

I’m pretty sure the PostgreSQL experts reading this wouldn’t be surprised by this crash, but it surprised me a lot!

It sent me in a completely different direction. I built a working exploit using this type-confusion feature to exploit against security extensions deployed by managed PostgreSQL providers. That research eventually became a part of the Part 2 story.

For a while, I moved on and left this type-confusion question behind.

Roughly two weeks later, something completely unrelated brought me back to it.

Detour: Tomatoes and SQL Injection

Let me take a small detour. This Postgres article series is all about telling you my story in the end, isnt it ?

I do not remember the exact date, but during one of our runs or walks, my partner Bilge (Staff Machine Learning Engineer at EDB) and I were discussing second-order SQL injection in the PostgreSQL AI extensions and the possibility of tricking AI features of these extensions to hallucinate and produce malicious SQL queries.

That conversation led to chatting about .

I first learned about SQL injection around 2005, and God knows how many times I have exploited it since.

Twenty years later, most libraries and frameworks still rely heavily on string escaping to generate secure SQL queries, even though RDBMSs have a beautiful feature named prepared statements.

I studied them when I was a uni student, mostly to see what could still be exploited even if the target app uses prepared statements. Things like triggering excessive SQL cold parsing and stuff like that.

But more importantly, for years I taught SQL Injection to thousands of my trainees with this concept:

In my version, the SQL query is the recipe and the values are the ingredients. Prepared statements let the database understand the recipe first, then receive the ingredients separately. So even a value like may look evil, but it remains data and never gets the chance to rewrite the query.

I had always seen this separation as a security feature. But this time, I noticed something in the middle of the convo with Bilge. Databases can finish all the parsing first and wait for me to execute it. Before execution, I can run whatever query I want.

I can alter types before executing the query!

Uncovering 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive

So the idea is simple; I could prepare a query, change something, and execute it later. But change what? PostgreSQL is not gonna let me redefine what the built-in types , , or mean.

I was not thinking about composite types at this point. Honestly, I barely knew what they were. I asked Claude agent pg_expert a much simpler question:

Which PostgreSQL types can I create, use inside a prepared query, and then alter it before running execute ?

That question led me to composite types. In PostgreSQL, a composite type represents the structure of a row. It is essentially a custom, user-defined data type that acts as a container for multiple fields, each with its own name and data type. [1, 2]

It had its own type OID, but its attributes defined the current row layout. I can change the attribute a type from UUID to another type without replacing the composite type itself.

I created a one-field composite where the attribute started as UUID. Then I prepared a query, changed that attribute to bytea, and executed the prepared statement.

And the result was a segfault!

I knew I had found exactly the kind of type confusion I had been looking for!

I knew this was no longer a superuser-only LANGUAGE internal behaviour I had exploited before.

I knew that I could trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role on any PostgreSQL instance. Probably all the Postgres-compatible offerings too (more about this later)

Last but not least, I already knew that controlled bytes reaching the wrong native consumer, in my case, had serious exploitation potential. These two have the most reliable exploit primitive I have seen in the PostgreSQL exploits.

Before diving into the Hacking PostgreSQL internals, we need to learn a few things about PostgreSQL to better understand the rest of the article!

Quick Course: What is BYTEA ?

is PostgreSQL’s data type for storing arbitrary binary data. Internally, it uses a variable-length representation called . PostgreSQL places a small header before the bytes to describe their size and storage format.

The header tells PostgreSQL which representation it is looking at and how large the complete value is.

We do not need to understand every representation. For the rest of this article, we only need to know two things

For example, a normal inline example of the five ASCII characters . That 24 can be decoded as which is 9. So 4-byte header + 5-byte payload = 9 bytes!

The most important example, external representation, when header starts with PostgreSQL believes the value is not stored inline at all. Instead, it treats the bytes as a reference to an expanded object somewhere in memory.

So the following data after the header is just object reference pointer instead of the data itself.

Crash and Root Cause Analysis

Lets get back to where we were.

The UUID I supplied contained exactly sixteen bytes, starting with and . While attribute a was still UUID, there was nothing special about or the fourteen zero bytes following it. They were simply controlled UUID data.

When we EXECUTE the query, PostgreSQL need to return the value of our type pg_temp.poc, in order to do that, it calls the composite output function, record_out().

So looks at the  pg_temp.poc’s attribute and says ‘That is bytea’ and selects

But the data    takes is our old UUID bytes that we can control. This is where the type confusion happens!

All of these means, we can literally create any representation we want by fully controlling the headers and following 12 byte!

Before could print the value, it first needed to convert this external representation into something it can print. I learned that PostgreSQL calls this process .

The exploitation idea: replacing NULL with our fake object that could make PostgreSQL follow to our own choosen methods!

Hijacking control-flow via Fake ExpandedObjects contains Native Function Pointers

ExpandedObjectMethods contains two native function pointers

Normal code uses those methods like this to convert an expanded object into its flat representation whenever it’s needed.

This is not normally an attacker-controlled callback interface. These are trusted internal representations created by PostgreSQL. The output functions can assume the pointer, header, and methods table are not malicious.

These are indirect native function calls. PostgreSQL obtains the function addresses from the object’s methods table and then calls them. That is something we can actually use to change the control-flow path.

Before going further, I needed a simple model for the objects involved. I named the two fake objects according to what they represented

So our plan is that the pointed to , pointed to , and contained the native function addresses that we wanna cal.

The important detail is that PostgreSQL used twice. Lets remember the actual C code

First, it treated as an and read the pointer at offset .

That pointer led to , where we had placed the address of . PostgreSQL then called the selected method and passed the original object pointer, , as its first argument.

In other words, H helped PostgreSQL find , and then the same H was handed to as its parameter.

Fortunately, the first eight bytes of H came before the pointer. I could place the NULL-terminated command in those bytes while keeping the address of at offset .

Leaking Memory Addresses and defeating the ASLR with the same primitive

As I have heavily talked about exploiting extensions vulnerabilities on managed-Postgres providers at Part 1, we dont get to read due to hardening. Our exploitation plan is very clear but the challenge is we need to leak addresses of these objects.

I started to chatting with my to find more about PostgreSQL operation that could return a pointer-valued data while SQL expected an ordinary integer. The moment I prompted the agent, it went to

It was a twist of fate. I had ended up exactly where the original idea had started.
