Normally, everything agrees:

The says its element is , so returns a pointer-valued text Datum and SQL processes it as text.

But what if the array internally says , while the surrounding SQL contract says ?

Because is passed by reference, returns a Datum containing the memory address of the text value! But the surrounding SQL expression expects a by-value , so PostgreSQL prints those same pointer bits as an integer.

In other to say this, we can exploit exactly same type confusion vulnerability to alter the arrays’ text element type to bigint so that unnest() will return the memory address instead of the value! aka leaking memory address!

Creating a PostgreSQL Array data structures with UUID

The smallest PostgreSQL Array needs 48 bytes. A single UUID gives a 16 controlled bytes. So we can simply combine 3 UUIDs next to each other to build exactly 48 byte fully controlled data structer!

The animation above shows how three UUIDs become one 48-byte array carrier. I prepare those bytes while all three attributes are still UUIDs. From there, I exploit the same type confusion for only the first UUID to !

So extracts the element as and returns its pointer, while SQL expects a and exposes that pointer as a memory address. The final skips the text header and lands on my controlled payload.

A direct to confusion would only reinterpret the old text bytes as an integer. The array was important because it forced PostgreSQL to first produce a real pointer and then expose those same pointer bits as a .

CVE-2026-6460 Umbrella Fix and Variant Analysis of 21 more cases

Once I have reached that point, I started thinking about different scenarios of where we can alter the attribute types before execution. All the other possible ways of keeping the old value alive.

I found the same underlying mistake around , conversion caches and different places.

I reported in total.

9 November 2026 The PostgreSQL security commits landed as part of a much larger release containing 52 new CVE.

are directly connected to this article.

  • is the main umbrella fix for type confusion. It introduces composite attribute versioning,
  • anonymous RECORD descriptors.
  • backend-local anonymous-RECORD typmod
  • statistics import could publish values under an obsolete type
  • prevents ExecEvalFieldStore[De]Form from using a mismatched
  • integer overflow in tuple-size calculation

Coordinating this with managed-PostgreSQL Providers

The reason why I have fallen into that rabbit hole 5 months ago was because I needed to better understand the how managed-database industry works before making a decision because at the end of the day, we all can outsource the infrastructure but we can not outsource the risk.

So I ported the my locally working exploit to almost every managed PostgreSQL platform I know and privately shared reproducible PoCs with their security teams.

I haven’t seen any vendor who is not affected by this vulnerability! including those who has Postgres compatible offering.

security team engineers validated all the exploits immediately. Thanks to Aaron and his team.

Google escalated the reports to its highest priority P0. I am genuinely grateful of all the support from Google Cloud VRP team since day one!

team received the full details around mid August. Thanks to endless support from the Etienne since I first contacted him.

Ubicloud members reached out to me after my part 1 article published and then they introduced me with the ClickHouse team. Both parties are also read in somewhere at end of August.

and Microsoft Azure PostgreSQL teams received the reports and working PoC at mid August.

But what I respected the most is that some vendors brought their most senior engineering members to start implementing their own mitigation. They did not want to leave customers exposed while waiting for the upstream release cycle.

So yeah my whole August was like that.

Closing: Thank you PostgreSQL Communities and Core Security Team

I spent 20 years of my life around security communities around the globe. But I really need to say that the support, positive approach and the respect I have seen my time at PGCONF.eu this year was quite suprized me. Have no idea PostgreSQL community at europe has such a family kind vibe.

After my talk “Nobody Gets to Be Superuser (Until I Broke In)” at PGCONF.eu last month Valencia, I have received amazing support from everyone, specially the respected members of the community who are effortlessly fixing these vulnerabilities whenever someone sends an email to the securit@ address.

I owe so much of where I am today to open source. I’ve spent my life learning by hacking things, understanding how they work, and making them more secure. Being able to contribute to PostgreSQL and its ecosystem in my own way means a lot to me. Seeing those contributions so warmly welcomed means even more.

My talk this year was not recorded upon my request, but I receive a lot of invitation from different countries for their local PostgreSQL meetups.

If you’d like to hear the whole story, I’ll be presenting the 90 minutes edition of it at the Prague PostgreSQL Meetup on Monday, 30 November.

(If you’ve made it this far, I’d love to hear your thoughts! Feel free to leave a comment or ask me anything.)

Appendix: Dating the Primitive and the Duplicate Fiesta

The mutable-row-type primitive dates to commit , introduced on May 5, 2004 with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE.

The exploitation technique I used relies on commit , introduced on May 14, 2015, which added expanded-object pointers and their native method callbacks. Later than many other primitives I discovered during exploiting 20+ variants.

I am not claiming that CVE-2026-6460 is exclusively “my vulnerability.” PostgreSQL treated it as an umbrella issue covering a much wider family of composite-type problems. Its commit credits many researchers whose reports may have involved overlapping discoveries, separate variants, or completely different journeys into the same systemic weakness.

That is the reality of vulnerability research in the age of AI. This article only tells the story of how I reached it without any cyber enabled models back in August 2026.

items.title: Our software engineering interviews are changing a little
items.author: maitland
items.content:
Over the last few years, LLMs have changed how software gets built and that’s no different for us at Jane Street. Most of our engineers now use them every day not only for writing code, but also for reading, debugging, and reviewing code, and plenty of things that aren’t code at all.

Our coding interviews haven’t changed, though. The questions we ask software engineers today are the same style of question we’ve been asking for years: sit down with an interviewer or two, program through a problem together, and talk as you go.

That style has served us well and the key goals remain the same: we want to see how you solve problems, structure your work, communicate, and collaborate in the pursuit of excellent software development. But the shape of the job has evolved, and we think our interviews should evolve, too. As generating code has become arguably cheaper than ever, other parts of the job have come to matter even more: taste about what to build, choosing abstractions that last, and making sure what got built is actually correct, among other things.

So this summer we started trialing some new kinds of interviews in our onsites for campus candidates. Broadly, they involve less code-writing, and lean more higher-level, focusing on software design, on verifying the quality, structure, and intention of code, and on using LLMs to produce code. Most rounds will continue to be traditional coding interviews, conducted without LLM assistance.

We know this sounds vague, but that’s intentional: the formats are still evolving, and we’d rather not describe something in detail today that looks different in six months.

A few things worth knowing:

  • Not every onsite includes these new rounds yet, and when you come on-site we’ll give you a heads-up about what to expect.

  • While we find LLMs incredibly valuable as part of our daily work, we also recognize that not everyone has deep experience working with them. You shouldn’t feel like you need to have a highly worked out methodology for working with agents in order to do well in our process. In the end, we’re looking for people with great instincts for building software, and we don’t feel like we need an LLM to evaluate that.
  • Different folks have integrated LLMs into their workflows in different ways and to different degrees, and we don’t expect you to have a particular setup or to use them for everything. What we care about is that you think clearly about the tools you use: what they’re good at, where they fall short, and when to reach for something else.
  • As has been the case for some time, our more experienced candidates’ interviews will continue to be more varied, featuring a range of interview styles, from producing software to designing systems and discussing prior work.

As always, we’ll keep iterating, and we’ll write more when there’s more to say.

items.title: The Utah Teapot
items.author: cobbal
items.content:
The has been the symbol of computer graphics. It was one of the first computer graphics models created using Bézier patches. This is the official Utah Teapot page, where you can you can visualize and download any of these historical versions or customize it, using the settings above.

Terms of Use and Attribution:The Utah Teapot model files are freely available for any use, including commercial use. To preserve the historical identity and provenance of the model, users are requested to identify the model, and any substantially derived version of it, as a (or ) and to acknowledge its origin as the historic Utah Teapot developed at the University of Utah. This request is intended solely to preserve the historical identity of the Utah Teapot and is not intended to restrict use of the model. The model files are provided “as is,” without warranty of any kind. The provider of these files shall not be liable for any claims, damages, or other liability arising from their use.

The Utah Teapot was originally created by Martin Newell and went through a number of modifications over the years. It quickly became famous within the graphics community after making its first appearance at SIGGRAPH in 1976. Its extensive use in graphics prompted Arvo and Kirk [1987] to name it the “Teapotahedron” and jokingly call it “the sixth Platonic solid”. It remains one of the standard models for evaluating new computer graphics algorithms and frequently appears in technical papers presented at SIGGRAPH and other graphics conferences. Utah Teapot has also appears in art installations, movies, video games, and a wide range of other graphics applications. Versions of the Utah Teapot model are included in numerous rendering and modeling programs and graphics APIs, among them 3ds Max, Direct3D, Houdini, Modo, OpenGL, POV-Ray, Quartz Composer, and RenderMan. See the Wikipedia page on the Utah Teapot.

Version 1975 - Martin Newell

This is the original version created by Martin Newell, while he was a PhD student at the University of Utah, by approximating the proportions of a physical teapot (Melitta by Friesland Porzellan). It is formed by 28 cubic Bézier patches, which he first drew the control points on an engineering paper. It is one of the first computer graphics object modeled using a set of nonlinear surfaces, rather than a collection of polygons. Notably, Martin Newell's version is taller than the commonly known shape of the famous Utah Teapot, and it has no bottom. This is the model that appeared in his dissertation, titled “The utilization of procedure models in digital image synthesis” in 1975, along with the rest of the tea set he modeled, though he prepared these models earlier, sometime in 1974.

Martin Newell's drawing of the Teapot and the tea set image from his dissertation.

Jim Blinn, while he was a PhD student at the University of Utah, scaled Martin Newell's teapot model by 3/4 during a demo. He liked its new shape and kept it that way. In fact, everyone liked this shorter version, including Martin Newell. Since 1976, this version of the teapot appeared in numerous publications, turning it into a symbol of computer graphics.

Utah Teapot was first introduced to the computer graphics community at SIGGRAPH 1976 in an article by Jim Blinn and Martin Newell, titled “Texture and Reflection in Computer Generated Images” (PDF). It was also published in the Communications of the ACM journal and an image from this article, featuring the Utah Teapot with a texture mapped to its patches, was used as the cover of the October 1976 issue.

Jim Blinn explains the components of the teapot and why it was squished in an article titled “What, Teapots Again?” (PDF), published in IEEE Computer Graphics & Applications in September 1987. There, he also suggests adding a flat bottom cap.

The cover of the CACM journal in October 1976, featuring one of the images from Blinn and Newell's paper at SIGGRAPH 1976, and two other images from the same paper with the original pixels computed on PDP-11 (after tone mapping) by Jim Blinn.

Version 1987 - Frank Crow

The most common version of Utah Teapot that appears in numerous graphics applications is the one released by Frank Crow, who was another PhD graduate of the University of Utah, in an article titled “The Origins of the Teapot” (PDF), published in IEEE Computer Graphics & Applications in January 1987. This article discusses the important role that the Utah Teapot model played in the early days of computer graphics and includes the control points of the scaled model by Jim Blinn. Except that all control points are shifted up just a bit to make room for a round bottom surface, defined by 4 additional Bézier patches. This brings the total number of patches to 32 and the total number of control points to 512.

Crow's figure showing the patch boundaries and the control polygon of the Teapot without its body, but with the bottom that he added.

Version 1992 - Hank Driskill

The handle and the spout patches of the original Utah Teapot model intersect with its body. This was necessary, as it was modeled using cubic Bézier patches. This was also a useful feature for testing various hidden surface removal algorithms that were being developed at the time, and their abilities in rendering intersecting surfaces. Also, because cubic Bézier patches cannot form perfectly circular shapes, the teapot's body was not perfectly round. Perhaps more importantly, it did not contain an interior and a rather visible gap around the lid.

In 1992, Hank Driskill, another PhD student at the University of Utah, addressed all these problems. He used the Alpha_1 software, which was being developed by Professors Elaine Cohen and Rich Riesenfeld and their students/collaborators, and he prepared a trimmed NURBS model of the Utah Teapot, connecting its perfectly round body to its handle and spout, and a new interior surface. Its bottom was flat, as suggested by Jim Blinn, instead of the round bottom that was previously added by Frank Crow. Nonetheless, Hank Driskill's design, titled “Utah, the Next Generation,” featuring this new Utah Teapot (with warp nacelles), won the SIGGRAPH 1992 T-Shirt Contest.

*Hank Driskill's version used a thick curve to cut a path through the spout. Here, we use the spout interior designed by Russ Fish instead.

The interior of this version was defined by revolving B-spline curves, resulting in 86 additional patches, so this version of the Utah Teapot has 118 patches in total.

Driskill's Teapot images with his new model and warp nacelles, and the award-winning t-shirt at SIGGRAPH 1992.

The version by Hank Driskill was later improved by Russ Fish, a co-founder and technical lead of the Alpha_1 project at the University of Utah. Russ Fish modeled a new interior with a hollow knob for the lid and presented his “third-generation” teapot at SIGGRAPH 2006 with the title “Teapot Subdivision.” He also released and documented this new and earlier versions of the Utah Teapot. In particular, his solution for generating the interior of the spout is elegant and closely follows the exterior contours prepared by Martin Newell. Similar to Hank Driskill's version, this one also has a flat bottom, rather than the round bottom of Frank Crow's version.

The "Teapot Subdivision" image generated by Russ Fish.

This version forms even more patches to model the interior, resulting in 134 patches in total.

Version 2026 - Cem Yuksel

The latest version of the Utah Teapot is prepared by Prof. Cem Yuksel of the University of Utah. This version uses much fewer patches for modeling the Teapot's interior and more closely follows the contours of its exterior. It contains a solid knob for the lid. The spout interior is also slightly modified to ensure that the surface normals are continuous where the tip of the spout meets the interior surface.

The new interior design works with both the round bottom of Frank Crow's model and the flat bottom used by Hank Driskill and Russ Fish. The official version has a round bottom, so that it matches the most commonly used form of the Utah Teapot today.

In addition, this latest version also includes two types of modifications to the exterior surface of the Utah Teapot:

  • Its original spline models are modified using a new continuity enhancement method to ensure curvature continuity. This ensures that the reflections on the teapot appear smooth, without the sharp changes that appear in the earlier versions. See the SIGGRAPH 2026 paper on this topic by Cem Yuksel, titled “Continuity-Enhancing Degree Elevation and Splits” for more information.

  • It also includes small chamfers where the spout and the handle meet the Teapot's body, ensuring that the teapot's surface normal is continuous over the exterior surface. The actual physical teapot that Martin Newell used as a reference has much larger chamfers, but adding such larger chamfers would deviate too much from the historical shape of the digital model.

The lightweight interior model of this version only needs 30 additional patches, so the resulting teapot has 62 patches in total.

Cem Yuksel also added texture mapping layouts that can be applied all versions of the Utah Teapot to achieve a bijective or a lower-distortion injective mapping.

items.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
items.author: zerop
items.content:
Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query.

As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution — a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs — rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs — is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently.

In Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions, a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) — once, offline, for a fixed database of keys — that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs.

A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into clusters — is typically much smaller than the total number of keys — keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has keys and evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of / — a factor-of- speedup when compared to the comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in Figure 1 below.

What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the support function of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, input convex neural networks (ICNNs). Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself.

The broad idea behind this work is to a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input.

If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best:

The neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality.

models learn to output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Euler’s theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced.

Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter.

As shown in Figure 1, the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each cluster’s centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match.

If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in Figure 2, in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings.

Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output scores at once. We can then use the largest of these scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: “How good is the key inside this cluster for this query?” SupportNets are trained in a classic machine learning fashion, also known as regression: we generate sample queries that are drawn from the distribution (typically embeddings for text queries), compute the ground-truth support functions at those queries, and train a neural network to replicate these values.

We trained SupportNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L → 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) on Natural Questions partitioned into 128 clusters. Natural Questions is a retrieval benchmark that pairs general-knowledge questions with passages from a large document database, roughly 2.6M unique passages in our setup.

Figure 4 below shows the retrieval performance in terms of recall as a function of different notions of cost. Routing recall is the fraction of queries whose true partition, the one holding the exact best key, lands among those the router chooses to probe. For both plots, an exhaustive search is carried out in the top- clusters matched with the query, where grows as powers of two . Naturally, all methods reach a recall of 1 when they survey all 128 clusters.

The first tab shows that for a fixed retrieval performance the learned routers reach it at lower latency than centroid routing. The small SupportNet model hits 95% routing recall about 1.9× faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and gains are even greater with the large model, which hits 97% in 1.74 ms. This plot explicitly factors in the additional compute incurred by running our small NNs rather than simply comparing to centroids.

The plot on the second tab looks exclusively at routing quality, neglecting the overhead incurred by running NNs. At a fixed budget of explored clusters, they find the right partition more often: scanning just 5% of the database, the learned routers recover the true partition ~90–93% of the time — up to 92.6% for the mid-size (M) — versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline.

SupportNet routing replaces the simple centroid-based routing found in existing inverted file index (IVF) systems. With KeyNet, we can also keep the IVF system as is and just feed it a modified version of the query. In that scenario, KeyNet works naturally as a in front of a standard approximate search index: predict where the best match is likely to be in embedding space, then ask your favorite IVF system to look there instead of starting from the original query. Because the IVF index is highly optimized, it can find the result faster when assisted by KeyNet. We also rely on regression to train KeyNets, as summarized in Figure 5: sample queries are matched with their ground-truth, best-matching key, and the KeyNet neural network is trained to reproduce that association.

We evaluated KeyNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L → 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) and in Figure 6 below, we show recall–cost tradeoffs for these different sizes. On the first tab, the search budget is wall-clock latency: reaching 99% recall takes up to ~8× less time with the largest model (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms for the raw query). As before, the second tab focuses exclusively on the boost in “quality” provided by replacing the original query with its KeyNet transformation. The x-axis is the fraction of the database the index actually scans: scanning just 0.001% of the database, KeyNet-mapped queries retrieve the true key 89–97% of the time — up to 96.7% for the largest model (L) — versus 86% for the raw query, and reaching 99% recall takes up to ~11× fewer keys (0.009% vs 0.10% raw). Better recall for the same cost, or the same recall for a fraction of it.

We show examples obtained from the same Natural Questions dataset discussed previously, served through a FAISS IVF index. It is one of several datasets we studied, and the trend is consistent across them. Querying the index with KeyNet’s predicted key consistently beats querying with the raw question, across the full search-budget sweep.

Namely, Figure 7 below shows five Natural Questions examples: top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query.

The choice between the two ends up being a practical one. Use when inference speed is the bottleneck and you just need to approximate the best key. Use when you also want a calibrated score (for re-ranking, thresholding, or downstream use), or when compute is tight at small model sizes — a regime where SupportNet stays competitive. Both train similarly, integrate with existing approximate-search infrastructure, and are reasonably robust to mild distribution shift in the query patterns. Ultimately, a very large-scale MIPS system for which the set of keys is huge may require both: train a SupportNet router over all clusters, and then one KeyNet per cluster to help its regular indices zero in on the best key faster.

Amortized MIPS reflects a shift in how retrieval can be approached when query distributions are known in advance — a common condition in production ML systems. By encoding MIPS solutions directly into network weights, the approach trades a one-time training (so-called ) cost for fast, lightweight inference and opens a practical path toward learned retrieval systems explicitly tailored to the queries they serve.

items.title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
items.author: linsomniac
items.content:
Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine

Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex on another machine — with all context intact. Install, then run

Over the past year or two, how I use my terminal has changed dramatically. For years I was the sole user of my shell, and everything in my Atuin history was authored by me. Now, more than half the commands running on my machines weren’t written by me.

These days, much of my work happens through a coding agent, typed into a little “Topsy-turvying” text box. But while my shell history follows me everywhere, my agent sessions do not. They're scattered across different tools and machines (a laptop, a dev server, ephemeral instances on exe.dev, a surprisingly cheap bare metal box in Germany), difficult to search, and often forgotten once I've moved on.

I started working on Atuin because the history of my work was ephemeral: every command I typed was destined to vanish on line 501 of . But once this work became indexed, everlasting, and easy to recall, I could find the exact command I’d used to fix something years ago, in seconds.

Over the years, this data compounded. It became the history of all of my work, the record of how I solved problems and built things.

Shell history has always been an excellent record of what happened, but it’s only the surface. It never kept the reasoning… or the intentions behind what I was trying to do. I could only find a command if I remembered a part of it, though often I remembered what I was trying to achieve more readily.

Agent sessions store the lot of it. Every command, its output, my intent, and everything I tried along the way to the eventual solution. It’s all there, in plain English, in my home directory! But just as with shell history all those years ago, we don’t put it to work.

That is why we built Atuin Threads.

Starting with Atuin 18.24, you can search your agent sessions across machines, resume them anywhere, or fork the session into a different agent harness. Start something in Claude Code on a dev server, then finish it in Codex on your laptop.

Behind the scenes, this was a natural extension of Atuin. We put a lot of time and effort into building a reliable, encrypted sync engine. It’s generic, and can sync anything that can be modelled as an append-only log. As it turns out, most AI sessions are exactly this.

Like shell history, Threads is end-to-end encrypted when synced, so we can't read your sessions. You can use our hosted sync server, run your own, or keep everything local. Capturing agent sessions is opt-in, too.

Run , and after setting up, you will see the TUI from the top of this post!

It doesn’t matter which agent you started with - you can resume it anywhere. With Atuin’s sync, this works across devices, and keeps your history backed up forever.

    with more agents coming soon.

    With MCP, agents can search and reference previous sessions themselves. They can find work you’ve done before, understand why a decision was made, and build on previous investigations without having to dig up the context.

    Our MCP is available as , and can be automatically installed with

    atuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode

    There are all sorts of ways to put this history to work. A few examples:

    I’ve iterated on our onboarding and setup so many times over the past few months, but never quite been happy with it. When I ask an agent to work on onboarding now, it finds all my previous attempts, as well as why they had been abandoned and what can be done better.

    These sessions contain the code that never made it into , as well as my initial prompts and iteration. Subsequent agents can use this to figure out exactly what I want, without me having to write up a giant spec.

    With all the security issues going on in the industry recently, we rolled our keys as a precaution. One of the new object store keys did not have the correct permissions for avatar uploads! We didn’t notice straight away 😬

    My daily Sentry triage agent picked up on it, and traced the failure down to a command run earlier that day. I hadn’t gotten around to reading it yet, but prompting another agent with

    seeing some tigris avatar issues?

    led to the agent discovering the previous investigation, highlighting the cause, and developing the fix much faster than if it had done the whole thing from scratch.

    Forking threads across machines

    Before releasing Threads, I did some testing on a variety of machines and setups.

    One machine did not perform well. The agent investigating proposed that this was because of poor IO performance, but that it needed something with a faster disk to confirm.

    I forked the session onto my MacBook, and it continued from exactly where it left off. With the faster SSD, the investigation concluded that slow disk was only part of the story - we could speed up imports elsewhere, too.

    Once the benchmarks were complete, the thread running on the original machine could pull the results from the Mac and build a fix. I didn’t have to copy-paste anything or co-ordinate across machines, and the data is now part of the record of my work.

    While this is tremendously useful as a solo engineer, it gets even more interesting with a team.

    So much of what we do never makes it into Git, issue trackers, or documentation. The context behind that work ends up scattered across individual agent sessions. What if the rest of the team could learn from it too? What if we could hand off an agent thread just like a Git branch?

    We’re building opt-in session sharing for teams, and would love to hear from folks using agents day to day. If this sounds useful to you, please get in touch!

    While agents have radically changed my daily workflow, shell history isn’t going anywhere, and is arguably more useful than ever. Threads is an extension of the same idea that started Atuin in the first place - the history of your work should be useful, accessible, and yours to keep.

    Threads is out in Atuin 18.24+

    1. Install or update Atuin with curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://setup.atuin.sh | sh
    2. Run to get started
    3. Use the MCP with

    Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any questions or feedback!

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving?
items.author: gmays
items.content:
There’s an intuitive but simplified picture of reasoning: let a model think for longer, and it’ll be more likely to be correct. This aligns well with our human intuition: spend more time and effort on thinking and it’s more likely that we’ll arrive at a correct answer.

But this picture doesn’t seem to explain everything. During RL training, models learn to write longer chains of thought, and they get more accurate as they do. Yet if you take a trained model and force any one chain to run longer, it helps for a while, then stops helping. Sometimes the answer even gets , as if it’s overthinking. If a chain of thought were truly converging toward some optimum, more steps shouldn’t make it worse. So is it really the length of each chain that helps at inference time? Or is it something more subtle?

This post is my attempt to clarify this confusion (mostly for myself) by looking at reasoning as pathfinding through token space. We’ll see that RL maximizes the probability of finding a path from $x$ to $\Scal_x$, but individual paths are not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. As a bonus, this perspective clarifies some odd observations about reasoning models, like unfaithful chains of thought and reward hacking.

Reasoning as pathfinding#

Ask a reasoning model the same math problem ten times and you’ll get ten different chains of thought. Rather than thinking of reasoning as one mysterious process heading toward an answer, let’s think of it as pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses one of them with each sample.

Consider the problem: “what’s $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + 10$”? One solution is to add the numbers one at a time: 1, 3, 6, 10, and so on up to 55. Another way is to pair them from the outside in: $1 + 10$, $2 + 9$, $3 + 8$, $4 + 7$ and $5 + 6$ each make 11, and five pairs of 11 make 55. Both of these paths land on the correct answer, 55.

We can think about reasoning as following this general pattern. We are given a starting point, the prompt, which we’ll call $x$. We want to find a path $z$ that starts from $x$ and ends at a correct answer $y$. To tell whether a path lands in the right place, we assume we have a verifier $r(x, y)$ that returns 1 if $y$ is correct and 0 if it isn’t.

So given a starting point $x$, we want to find a path of tokens $z$ that lands in the set

$$\Scal_x = \{y : r(x, y) = 1\}.$$

The figure at the top of this post sketches this picture. Each gray line is a sampled path: it starts from the prompt on the left, meanders in token space by sampling $z$, with some of these paths landing in $\Scal_x$.

Since many paths land in $\Scal_x$, the success probability adds up over all of them. Let $\pi(z \mid x)$ be the probability that the model generates the path $z$ given the prompt $x$, and $y(z)$ for the final answer at the end of $z$. The probability of success is the probability of generating each path, times the probability that path lands in $\Scal_x$, summed over every path:

$$p_x = \prob{\text{a path lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = \sum_{z} \underbrace{\pi(z \mid x)}_{\text{samples path } z}\; \underbrace{\prob{y(z) \in \Scal_x \mid z}}_{\text{path } z \text{ lands in }\Scal_x}.$$

The second factor is just 1 if the path lands in $\Scal_x$ and 0 if it doesn’t, so we sum only the probability of paths that land in $\Scal_x$:

$$p_x = \sum_{z} \pi(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} = \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi(z \mid x).$$

We’ll call $p_x$ the . Maximizing this probability means our model will be more likely to sample a path that lands in $\Scal_x$.

Note that there are two ways of increasing this probability. Either the model can sample multiple paths to the same answer, each with a small probability, or the model can sample a single path to the answer with a very high probability. The success probability doesn’t care which one we get, but in practice we might want to prioritize specific paths or ensure diversity in the samples.

How do we boost our success probability?#

The simplest way to pathfind is to have the model $\pi$ keep sampling paths $z$ until one lands in $\Scal_x$.

Since we assumed we had a verifier, we can do best-of-$k$ sampling, which samples $k$ paths and looks for a success. Each path misses with probability $1 - p_x$, so all $k$ miss with probability $(1-p_x)^k$, and the success probability rises from $p_x$ to

$$\prob{\text{at least one of } k \text{ paths lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = 1 - \underbrace{(1-p_x)^k}_{\text{all } k \text{ paths miss}}.$$

This is a guaranteed axis of compute-scaling. As long as $p_x > 0$, the success probability increases monotonically as we sample more paths, so spending more compute on more samples always helps, as seen early on by Brown et al. 2024. However, the scaling here is over the number of samples rather than the length of the paths (thinking longer).

Train the model to generate better samples#

So far the model was fixed, so $p_x$ was fixed too. Can we change the model to increase $p_x$ itself?

Here’s a simple way to do this. Collect many prompts whose answers we can check. For each one, sample some paths from the model. We keep the paths that land in $\Scal_x$, and train the model on the ones we kept. Then repeat. Each round, we train the model to put more weight on the successful paths that it sampled. This loop is called rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and STaR was an early version of it for reasoning.

RL with a verifiable reward, which is how today’s reasoning models are trained, turns out to do almost the same thing. Let $\pi_\theta$ be the model with weights $\theta$. Then since $r(x, y(z)) = 1$ exactly when $y(z) \in \Scal_x$:

$$ \begin{aligned} p_x &= \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi_\theta(z \mid x) \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, r(x, y(z)) \\ &= \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))}, \end{aligned} $$

meaning the expected binary reward is exactly the success probability $p_x$.

Computing the gradient of the success probability via the log-derivative trick, we arrive at

$$\grad_\theta\, p_x = \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))\, \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z \mid x)},$$

which is exactly the policy gradient, also called the REINFORCE estimator. Now estimate this gradient with $N$ sampled paths $z_1, \dots, z_N$. The paths that failed have $r = 0$ and disappear, while the paths that land in $\Scal_x$ have $r = 1$. If $M$ of the $N$ paths succeed, the estimate is

$$\grad_\theta\, p_x \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x) = \underbrace{\frac{M}{N}}_{\text{success rate}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{M} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x)}_{\text{log likelihood of the successful paths}}.$$

This gradient involves two terms: the empirical success rate $M/N$ and the average log likelihood of the successful paths.

In other words, a step of REINFORCE with a binary reward is a step of rejection-sampling fine-tuning on the model’s own sampled paths, scaled by the current success rate $M/N$.

This also explains the first observation from the intro, that chains of thought get longer during RL training. Each step pulls the model toward the paths that landed, so if the paths that succeeded tended to be longer than the ones that failed (e.g. because they include backtracking behavior, gather more feedback from the environment, or just dumb luck), the model will learn to write longer paths.

Amortization and generalization#

During RL training, we spend a lot of compute to search for good paths and then we train the model to generate those paths directly. Once trained, the model can produce the answer without spending all this extra compute on sampling multiple paths. This is called the search: we pay for it once during training, so we don’t have to pay for it every time we ask the model a question. Since we train a on many prompts, the model can potentially to new prompts it has never seen.

The figure below shows this for four prompts, each with its own $\Scal_x$, and switches between the model before and after training. During training, we sample paths from every prompt, keep the ones that succeed, and SFT on them. The percentages show the empirical rate of success given each prompt. The hollow prompt is new and not seen before by the model, but the model generalizes to this new prompt after training. As the new prompt gets further from the training distribution, its accuracy drops (try dragging it!).

Revisiting some observations about reasoning#

Once we see a reasoning model as a distribution trained to land in $\Scal_x$ given any $x$, a few odd facts about these models become clear.

Chains of thought are not guaranteed to be faithful#

Our verifier above only checks whether the answer is correct. The reward is 1 if $y(z) \in \Scal_x$ and 0 otherwise, so the intermediate tokens $z$ are just a way for the model to get to the answer. Nothing requires those tokens to be true, or to explain the answer that follows, though of course these are often correlated due to the model’s pretraining.

If we want meaningful chains of thought, we need to adjust the rewards or the training objective.

We also assumed the verifier is never wrong, that $r(x, y)=1$ if and only if $y$ is actually the correct answer to $x$. But in practice the verifier can be imperfect. Then $\Scal_x$, the set of answers the verifier accepts, isn’t the same as the set of correct answers: it can include wrong answers and leave out correct ones. This misspecification opens up regions of $\Scal_x$ that the model might learn to land in even though it’s not what we intended.

Thus reward-hacking comes from an imperfect verifier, which fails to capture what we truly want, as well as an imperfect sampling procedure which fails to stay away from these shortcut regions.

In the figure below, the dashed circle is the set of correct answers and the red ellipse is $\Scal_x$. The ellipse stretches back toward the prompt, so its wrong answers are the easiest to reach, and after training most paths land there.

This visualization also shows why scaling up RL (generating more samples and longer samples) makes reward hacking more likely. The more extensively we “fuzz” the verifier, the more likely we’ll find a path that lands in the misspecified region of $\Scal_x$. Once the model finds this shortcut, training pushes the model towards similar behavior.

So what objective is reasoning solving?#

Reasoning isn’t actually solving any objective at all. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. It’s only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success.

RL training directly raises the success probability $p_x$, by spending a lot of compute on searching for successful paths and then training the model to reproduce them. Thinking longer helps because training taught the model to use the extra tokens, not because generating more tokens is intrinsically better. The cost of sampling during RL is amortized into the weights. At inference time the model is likely to succeed with a single sample, but any individual sample is not guaranteed to succeed.

items.title: A comprehensive study of how fingerprintable users are
items.author: tomrittervg
items.content:
Tom Ritter, Fatih Kilic, Frederik Braun, Elisa Luo, Geoffrey M. Voelker, Stefan Savage, Christoph Kerschbaumer

Mozilla Corporation  ·  University of Toronto  ·  UC San Diego

This is the companion site to a study Mozilla ran on browser fingerprinting. With the help of almost 25 million Firefox release users, we measured how identifiable browsers really are, found which characteristics make them unique, and used that to design the fingerprinting protections that shipped in Firefox 143. Here you can read the paper and its key findings, browse the full appendix data the PDF had no room for, download the privacy-preserving aggregate data and analysis code, learn how the data was collected, and run an interactive test that compares your own browser against the measured population. If you have a question the data could answer, there is also a discussion board for proposing follow-up research.

Browser fingerprinting is a known tracking mechanism on the modern web, but its real-world effectiveness toward users has been hard to measure. To build robust protections, we measured uniqueness across a large, unbiased population, to determined what individual metrics cause users to be unique. These measurements used multiple privacy preserving technologies, like , to ensure that no individual users can be identified or tracked across the web. The protections we built into Firefox avoid web compatibility problems while dropping the percentage of uniquely identifiable users from 75% to 46%.

Web browser fingerprinting has become a key tracking mechanism on the modern web, yet its real-world effectiveness and which of the existing mitigations offer value at scale remain insufficiently understood.

In this paper, we present a large-scale study of browser fingerprinting based on real-world telemetry from almost 25 million Firefox release users. This dataset enables us to quantify user uniqueness at population scale and identify which characteristics contribute most to this uniqueness.

Our analysis shows fingerprintability is largely driven by a small set of high-impact characteristics and their combinations, rather than the accumulation of many independent measurements. Building on these insights, we propose and evaluate fingerprinting protections based on their impact on uniqueness and cohort structure, and design data-driven mitigations.

These protections, shipped in Firefox 143, reduce the fraction of uniquely identifiable users from 75% to 46% while maintaining web compatibility, demonstrating that practical reductions in fingerprintability are achievable in a mainstream browser.

Here's what we want to present to you with this paper and the broader scope of our work.

Fingerprinting test sites have a seemingly endless list of measurements they can pull from your browser. If a user has a unique fingerprint, it is typically not because of a single measurement, but it is not because of 20 or 30 measurements. It is a small number of metrics that make users unique.

In fact, it's very close to the 80/20 rule. Specifically, of all the users seen as unique by Fingerprint Pro (the most discerning fingerprinter we model) - 80% of them are unique after only 8 metrics - while the fingerprinter collects a total of over 50 metrics. Signifyd collects more metrics, but identifies fewer users as unique: 80% of the users it sees as unique will be identified after 9 metrics despite collecting over 80.

Whenever someone cites a single percentage when describing "How many users are unique" - you should be suspicious. Because this collapses multiple different populations that behave very differently.

Firstly, as a baseline, your operating system is always going to be exposed to a fingerprinter. We are always working within the constraint of web compatibility, and lying about the user's operating system breaks shortcut keys and gives you the wrong downloads among other problems. So if we the website is going to learn your real OS anyway, we can use it to segment the population and analyze it separately.

And when you do you see that each operating system behaves differently because they have different important metrics. Admittedly, it's very difficult to give a concise summary of work and also provide four sets of numbers - so even we fall prey to the trap of providing a single number, as we did in the prior paragraph. But we have a single percentage, somewhere we have that number broken down by operating system, and in doing so, you will see that each behaves differently.

It's so, so easy to take all the results for a metric and just calculate Shannon entropy - it's a standard yardstick in this literature. But as we show - a high Shannon entropy does not reliably predict fingerprinting impact.

Previous analyses calculated how many people were unique, but they did not analyze the people - the ones who weren't. All those other people might be 1 million users who share one fingerprint or 500,000 distinct fingerprints shared by 2 people each - that's quite the difference.

We use the Simpson Index (aka the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index) to quantify that difference and compare different sets of cohorts (shared fingerprints). This lets us compare how effective different fingerprinting defenses are based not just on how much uniqueness they eliminate but how much they collapse groups of users into each other.

For example, two different protections can each lower the share of unique users by about 2.1 percentage points. But one improves the cohort score by 56%, while another raises it by only 13%. Judged on uniqueness alone, two defenses can look equally effective; while the cohort improvement varies significantly.

Protections are not uniformly impactful, and the variation is not small. As an example, clamping the available screen resolution takes 25.3 percentage points off cumulative macOS uniqueness but between 0 and 3 points off the other three platforms. Averaged across all users, that 25-point drop shrinks to 3.5 - a protection that matters enormously to one platform can look marginal in the aggregate.

This is yet another reason why it's so important to segment and analyze data on a per-operating-system basis.

Making users report the same values makes them look more alike, but it never makes everyone look the same. Some users will still stand out, and that gets worse on websites with small visitor populations. Standardization improves the situation, but it should still be paired with randomization. Randomization is very strong when it works, but can always be detected and bypassed. Neither can carry the burden of providing privacy on its own.

Correlating fingerprinting values with users' hardware and other characteristics let us identify why certain measurements differed between users. Knowing the root cause lets us build protections that reach much further, and protect small groups of users who would otherwise stand out as a minority.

Breakage from a strict mode is delayed, and the delay hides the cause. Turning on a stricter mode is a one-time act - but the broken website arrives later and nothing connects the two. From the user's perspective, this website doesn't work in Firefox and they have no idea why and are frustrated. Report after report we see people posting for help, confused - despite having taken specific action to enable a hidden setting opting them into strict fingerprinting protections.

Users don't realize that a setting they changed caused the breakage, and don't know how to fix it - so a protection that breaks the web breaks the browser along with it. We selected and tuned mitigations on both measured impact compatibility. For a default, compatibility isn't a trade-off against privacy - it's a precondition for it.

The web is vast, and even the most innocuous change is likely to break something somewhere. Some breakage can be anticipated, which helps design, testing, and detection. The other breakage gets fixed only if a chain of luck holds: someone has to recognize the breakage, report it, reproduce it on the right hardware, and get it to the right person.

Commercial fingerprinters evolve continuously, and they borrow openly from the community that studies them. Sites built to teach people about fingerprinting - CreepJS among them - get picked up and used outright by fingerprinting products.

So we have been deliberately conservative. There are analyses this dataset would support that we have not run, data we could have released that we have not, and offensive angles on this work that we have not pursued. That is a choice rather than an oversight: we would rather leave a question open than make it easier to build a better fingerprinter.

This interactive test re-implements individual measurements as close as possible to how Firefox's own collection code performed them, runs in your browser, and compares each result against the published aggregate data. For every characteristic you can see your value and how many of the ~25 million measured browsers share it - overall and within your operating system.

The test runs entirely in your browser. All comparisons happen locally, against our static reference files. No data is stored or submitted to us.

If the test, or anything else on this site, looks wrong, please report it as an issue on GitHub. For a problem with the test, include the diagnostics from its button, or, if you would rather not post your measured values publicly, email them to tom@ritter.vg.

The paper's appendices contain a wealth of data locked behind a reasonable page limit and PDF formatting. This full data page carries all of it - every rank for every operating system and all three modeled services, the complete protection chains, and the paper's figures regenerated at print resolution.

Our measurements come from Firefox telemetry, specifically the ping, a dedicated telemetry ping. Unlike normal telemetry pings that are sent regularly, this ping must be explicitly enabled (which has happened twice, once in 2025 and once in 2026), and sends one data report before becoming dormant again.

This ping carries no client ID, only a UUID unique to the ping used to de-duplicate users. It cannot be keyed to any other telemetry submissions. It is submitted over Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP): a relay operated independently of Mozilla forwards the encrypted submission, so the relay can see the sender's IP address but not the contents, and Mozilla receives the contents but not the IP address. Access to the collected data was restricted to four authorized Mozilla employees. The data was retained for 90 days and has since been deleted.

Aggregate data & analysis code

We release four types of data:

  1. A list of fingerprints generated for different phases of protections, per modeled fingerprinter, with the user's OS and locale unmasked.
  2. Aggregate tables of the frequency of value per metric, split by OS
  3. Aggregate tables of the frequency of value per metric, correlated by other metrics' values, again split by OS
  4. A detailed analysis of rendered canvas images that allows comparison

In the fingerprint lists, the fingerprints cannot be recreated from a website measuring user characteristics, due to the way the telemetry was collected. After being generated, the files were shuffled to a new ordering, and any locale occurring fewer than 100 times was anonymized.

In the aggregate tables, any value observed fewer than 100 times within a single per-OS population is withheld - so the published data describes cohorts, never individuals.

In the canvas comparison, raw canvas renderings are provided, but they are devoid of any connection to other user data. Any unique canvas rendering is not provided; only the hash.

For verification and exploration, the code used to process the data and perform different analyses is available for review. It additionally contains the specific fingerprinting scripts captured, reverse engineered, and modeled for the paper.

Far more can be asked of this dataset than we have asked. Some of it we chose not to pursue, some of it we simply did not think of, and some of it is a better fit for someone who is not us.

There is a discussion board for proposing follow-up analyses. Two kinds are worth posting:

  • Answerable from the published aggregate data. Anyone can run these - the per-operating-system distributions are released, and the analysis toolkit is open. Post the question anyway, so the work is not duplicated and so the result lands somewhere others can find it.
  • These we would have to run ourselves, since the underlying ping data is not something we can ever release. Describe what you want to know and why! To be clear, we do not have the raw data anymore but it is possible we will perform a re-collection in the future which we could analyze. We cannot promise to run everything, and some questions we will decline because we do not wish to help build a better fingerprinter.

items.title: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast
items.author: pixelpoet
items.content:
Hello you fine Internet folks,

Today we’re looking at AMD’s next-generation Zen 6 CPU core family. We’ll explore the changes from Zen 5 and what the differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c tell us about AMD’s approach to microarchitecture.

At a high level the changes AMD made to the integer schedules stand out, returning to a layout reminiscent of Zen 3 and Zen 4.

Zen 5 had the best direction predictor of any core we have measured and Zen 6 seemingly builds upon that same direction predictor.

Zen 6 has also improved the ability of the core to do 2 branches per cycle with Zen 6 able to do 2 branches per cycle within the L1 instruction cache.

When the footprint exceeds the L1i, then it falls to just a single branch per cycle for the rest of the BTB except for the 64B test which goes up to 4 cycles per branch for the L2 BTB.

When comparing the BTB of Zen 6 to Zen 5, Zen 6 appears to have focused on improving the speed of the BTB compared to beefing up the capacity.

The accuracy of Zen 6’s Branch Predictor Unit is very similar to Zen 5’s while also being faster which is a good thing considering that Zen 5 already had a very accurate Branch Predictor.

Zen 6 carries forward the same dual decode cluster schema that Zen 5 introduced but, unlike Zen 5 where a single thread could only effectively use a single decode cluster, now with Zen 6 a single thread can use both decode clusters.

Outside of the L1i, Zen 6 looks very similar to Zen 5’s behavior on the instruction side of things.

The execution engine of Zen 6 is overall very similar to Zen 5, but there are some important differences to be mindful of.

On the integer side, Zen 6 brings back Zen 4’s NOP pairing behavior, retiring up to 16 NOPs per cycle. Zen 6 also comes closer to theoretical peak throughput for simple integer instructions than Zen 5, sustaining 5.96 64-bit adds per cycle against Zen 5’s 5.25 with the same six ALUs.

AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. According to AMD, Zen 5’s third integer multiply unit did not justify its area cost.

On the vector side, the floating-point units are unchanged, with Zen 6 still handling two 512-bit FADDs, FMULs, or FMAs per cycle. The change is in VNNI, where Zen 6 doubles the number of units from two to four and our 512-bit VNNI test goes from 1.99 to 3.88 instructions per cycle, with Zen 6c matching it. VNNI instructions are useful for operations like calculating the inner loop of quantized inference as well as for video codecs using them for video filters as well.

Moving over to the other notable change, Zen 5 could already perform four per cycle, but our test shows only two of them could be vector loads, regardless of if they were 256 or 512 bit loads. Zen 6 raises 256-bit loads to four per cycle on both cores while leaving 512-bit loads at two, so both widths now reach the same 128 bytes per cycle which matters because most shipped vector code still targets AVX1/2.

In the past the difference between the Classic cores and the Dense cores in terms of the architecture were, for all intents and purposes, functionally identical with the biggest changes being in the number of cores on a CCD and the amount of L3 cache per core. With the Zen 6 family, that has changed.

Starting inside of the core, the changes occur after micro-op dispatch and seemingly end after the load queue.

The main differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c lie in the capacities of their out-of-order structures. Several of these structures are larger on Zen 6c, allowing it to keep more work in flight and absorb more latency than Zen 6. The reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, the integer register file from 288 to 352, the vector scheduler from 138 to 180, and the load queue from 280 to 330.

The differences suggest that AMD is specializing the two designs. Zen 6 appears tuned for high frequency, while Zen 6c has more capacity to tolerate comparatively high memory latency.

Zen 6 and Zen 6c use 12-core and 32-core CCDs, respectively, but both provide 4 MB of L3 cache per core. That gives the 12-core CCD 48 MB of L3 cache and the 32-core CCD 128 MB.

L3 latency has increased from about 47 cycles on Zen 5 to 55 cycles on Zen 6 and 66 cycles on Zen 6c. The larger caches and greater number of mesh stops likely contribute to the increase. In nanoseconds, Zen 6’s higher clock hides most of the increase, at 10.7 ns against 10.3 ns on the Zen 5-based EPYC 9355P, while Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger CCX put it at 16.4 ns.

Moving over to bandwidth, we see that Zen 6 fixes Zen 5’s odd L2 bandwidth behavior, where a core pulled only about 42 bytes per cycle across most of the L2’s capacity, in Zen 6 the read path now reliably delivers 64 bytes per cycle. The rest of the cache hierarchy is largely unchanged in bandwidth per cycle.

Store-to-load forwarding is seemingly unchanged from Zen 5 and is where the behavior of Zen 6 and Zen 6c re-unify.

A 32-bit load from the same address as a 64-bit store completes with effectively zero latency which lets Zen 6 handle two dependent store-load pairs per cycle. Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5.

The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3.

The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point.

The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian.

Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage.

Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point.

Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share.

The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips.

The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher.

Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.

The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.

The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy.

The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.

The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.

The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5.

However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior.

The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs.

AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs.

items.title: Announcing .NET 11
items.author: runesoerensen
items.content:
Today, we’re excited to announce the release of .NET 11! This year’s release

.NET 11 is a Standard Term Support (STS) release with under the .NET support policy. STS and Long Term Support (LTS) releases have the same quality and servicing policies; the difference is the length of support. .NET 10 remains a supported LTS option. Stay current with servicing updates whichever release you choose.

Join us at .NET Conf, November 10-13

Explore .NET 11 with the product teams and community at .NET Conf 2026. The conference includes product team sessions on November 10 and 11, followed by two days of community sessions.

Some of the changes we’re most excited for you to try:

  • C# 15 union types and closed hierarchies help you express the possible states of your application and handle them with compiler-checked patterns.
  • A Native AOT CLI host and a warm MSBuild server reduce overhead in everyday developer workflows.
  • ASP.NET Core brings asynchronous validation, OpenAPI 3.2, and new capabilities for Blazor and SignalR applications. Experimental Blazor AI components integrate with the Agent User Interaction Protocol (AG-UI) for advanced agentic web experiences.
  • Build AI-powered, agentic applications with Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) for model access, MCP for tool integration, and Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) for agents and workflows.
  • Put agentic development tools to work with .NET Skills for .NET-specific guidance, .NET MAUI DevFlow for inspecting and testing running apps, and the .NET Upgrade canvas for reviewing modernization progress.
  • .NET MAUI adopts CoreCLR as its default runtime and improves XAML iteration and native controls.
  • The libraries add built-in Zstandard compression, simpler process execution, richer JSON support, and new ways to work with in-memory data without copying it first.

C# 15 is the default language version for projects targeting .NET 11. Union types are one of its biggest additions: a value can be one of a declared set of case types, with conversions from those types and exhaustiveness checking in switch expressions.

Consider a product lookup that either finds a product or reports that it wasn’t found:

ProductLookup result = new Product(42, "Mechanical keyboard");

string message = result switch
{
    Product product => $"Found {product.Name}",
    ProductNotFound missing => $"No product with ID {missing.Id}",
};

Console.WriteLine(message);

public sealed record Product(int Id, string Name);
public sealed record ProductNotFound(int Id);
public union ProductLookup(Product, ProductNotFound);

The result type tells a caller which outcomes it needs to handle. There’s no need to use or an unrelated base class just to put those outcomes behind one return type.

C# 15 also adds . A class limits direct derivation to its declaring assembly, giving the compiler the information it needs to check patterns over the hierarchy. Unions are useful when you want to combine existing types; closed hierarchies fit models where you own the inheritance relationship.

Smaller language features help with everyday code, too. Collection expression arguments let you pass constructor or factory arguments without giving up collection expression syntax:

HashSet<string> names =
    [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "Alice", "ALICE", "Bob"];

Console.WriteLine(names.Count);

This prints : the comparer controls equality, so and are one entry.

Other additions include extension indexers and labeled and . These features don’t require the preview language version. The separate memory safety work ; see the C# 15 feature documentation for its opt-in requirements.

F# 11 improves compiler memory use and reduces allocations in FSharp.Core collection operations. It also adds ways to bound concurrent asynchronous work, useful when a collection operation would otherwise start more work than a service or machine can handle comfortably.

The F# release notes distinguish the default-language updates from preview capabilities, including Runtime Async support for custom computation-expression builders.

The SDK now enables a Native AOT CLI host by default. Commands such as help and version queries can run without starting the managed CLI, and tool launches can avoid that startup path too. Commands that need managed execution still use it.

The MSBuild server also stays warm between CLI invocations by default, reducing repeated startup work. SDK installers on Linux and macOS are smaller through assembly deduplication.

File-based apps can grow across source files with , and solution filters can be created and edited from the CLI. adds Aspire app-host integration, crash recovery, and device selection for mobile projects.

For teams using Microsoft.Testing.Platform, gains run-level timeouts, failure limits, clearer progress reporting, and per-module results directories. The test runner matters: these switches aren’t interchangeable with the VSTest command-line options.

Container publishing adds reproducible image digests through and avoids redundant layer uploads when the target manifest already exists. NuGet source configuration gains a minimum package publication age setting, which lets teams wait before newly published package versions become eligible for selection. This is an additional policy control, not a replacement for vulnerability checks or reviewing dependencies.

Performance work in .NET 11 reaches both the code you deploy and the tools you use to develop it. Stephen Toub’s Performance Improvements in .NET 11 takes a detailed tour through hundreds of runtime and library optimizations, with benchmarks and code examples.

The just-in-time (JIT) compiler improvements remove more redundant bounds checks and branches, improve devirtualization, and fold more operations into constants. For example, the JIT can optimize additional calls when it knows the inputs at compile time. These changes improve generated code without requiring you to rewrite the corresponding application logic.

Native AOT interface dispatch uses a shared helper that reduces the code needed at interface call sites and improves throughput for interface-heavy workloads. Hardware support also expands, including FP16 instructions for operations on supported x64 and Arm64 hardware and new vector construction and composition APIs.

There’s useful work on diagnostics, too. In-process crash report logging can capture a managed stack trace, module information, and runtime state before a process exits. Previously available on mobile platforms, this reporting path now also supports Linux and macOS.
