As always, measure the effect on your own application. Throughput, startup time, memory use, and deployment size depend on the workload and publishing options you choose.

Runtime Async has been a recurring theme throughout the .NET 11 previews. It moves asynchronous suspension and resumption into the runtime instead of relying on compiler-generated state machines.

One especially useful result is a clearer call stack. Profilers and debuggers can show the asynchronous methods themselves instead of the infrastructure used to execute them. This is a distinction from exception stack traces, which already hide much of that infrastructure.

Runtime Async remains a preview feature. To try it in a project targeting , add:

<PropertyGroup>
  <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>
</PropertyGroup>

You don’t need to enable for this scenario. The .NET runtime libraries themselves are built with Runtime Async, but opting your application’s code into the new compilation model is a separate choice. See the Runtime Async documentation for its behavior and current guidance, and test your application’s dependencies and diagnostics before adopting it.

The .NET 11 SDK includes an MCP server template. MCP gives AI applications a common way to discover and call tools and services. The template uses the official MCP C# SDK and includes a working sample tool, so you can start exposing your own functionality without first installing a separate template package:

dotnet new mcpserver -o MyMcpServer

For applications that consume AI services, Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) provides abstractions such as and . These libraries let you compose model access with dependency injection, caching, and OpenTelemetry using familiar .NET patterns. They’re available as NuGet packages, rather than features that require you to move all of your application code to a new framework version.

Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) builds on these abstractions with agents that call tools and maintain conversation state, plus workflows that coordinate agents and application code. Connect agents to MCP tools to give them access to your application’s capabilities, and expose an agent through an ASP.NET Core AG-UI endpoint to build an interactive Blazor experience. The AG-UI hosting integration is currently prerelease.

The .NET libraries add capabilities that previously required extra setup, intermediate buffers, or custom helpers.

The API expansion includes one-shot methods to run a process and capture its output and exit status. More advanced APIs give you control over inherited handles, suspended starts, and process signaling. Build tools and developer utilities can spend less code on process plumbing while still inspecting how a child process finished. See Process API Improvements in .NET 11 for examples.

Zstandard compression joins the existing compression formats in . New span-based compression APIs support callers that manage their own buffers, and ZIP improvements include CRC32 validation when reading entries.

Four new in-memory stream adapters bridge existing data to APIs that accept a : , , , and . For example, a pipeline’s segmented can be read as a stream without first flattening it into a new contiguous buffer.

adds support for C# unions, F# discriminated unions, and JSON Lines output from asynchronous sequences. F# union support uses reflection and doesn’t support source generation, trimming, or Native AOT, so check the documented limits before choosing it for a trimmed application.

LINQ adds , which preserves unmatched elements from both inputs. This is useful for reconciliation work, such as comparing two inventories where you need to see missing items on either side.

The libraries also expand numeric types, DNS resolution, cryptography, and tracing configuration. The library overview covers the complete set of changes and marks APIs that remain experimental.

EF Core removes unnecessary joins in more reference-navigation and split-query scenarios, improves translation, and translates the new LINQ operator on relational providers that support it. These changes can simplify generated SQL while letting more queries stay in LINQ.

Complex types and JSON columns can now be used on entities mapped with table-per-type or table-per-concrete-type inheritance. Other improvements include migrations tooling and additional provider-specific JSON capabilities.

For SQL Server applications, EF Core adds support for vector indexes and approximate vector search. The SQL Server features and corresponding EF APIs are experimental. See the vector search documentation and limitations before evaluating them.

EF Core 11 requires .NET 11. When upgrading, check your database provider’s compatibility and the EF Core 11 breaking changes as well as the runtime changes.

The new dotnetup toolchain manager lets you install and update .NET SDKs and runtimes in your user account. It’s currently in public preview and helps you manage side-by-side versions and keep up with servicing updates.

The experimental .NET MAUI DevFlow toolkit exposes a running app’s visual tree, screenshots, and interaction tools, so an agent can inspect and test the UI rather than work only from source code.

For modernization, the .NET Upgrade canvas gives you a visual view of a GitHub Copilot upgrade session. Review assessment findings and dependency compatibility, follow implementation tasks, and monitor failures and progress as the upgrade agent works. Our modernization walkthrough in the GitHub Copilot app covers the workflow from assessment through execution.

Web: ASP.NET Core and Blazor

Application types are most useful when the rest of the stack understands them. ASP.NET Core supports C# unions wherever it uses , including JSON request and response bodies in Minimal APIs and MVC. Generated OpenAPI documents describe the union’s alternatives with an schema.

This support applies to JSON bodies, not to route, query, header, or form binding. When multiple union cases have the same JSON shape, configure a classifier so deserialization can distinguish them. The ASP.NET Core union documentation explains those boundaries.

Validation also becomes more practical for rules that need to do I/O. Asynchronous validation works with the new asynchronous DataAnnotations APIs, so a validator can await a database lookup or a remote call instead of blocking a thread. Minimal APIs and Blazor forms can use this support.

OpenAPI 3.2 is now the default for generated documents. Among other improvements, it lets the document describe the per-event payload of a server-sent event stream. If a client generator or another part of your toolchain doesn’t yet support 3.2, you can explicitly select an earlier document version.

For long-lived connections, SignalR authentication refresh lets a connection refresh authentication without reconnecting. Blazor Interactive Server components can receive the updated identity and react when claims change.

Blazor adds capabilities for both statically rendered pages and interactive applications.

The new component caches the rendered output of a component subtree during static server-side rendering. On a cache hit, Blazor replays the markup without creating those child components or running their lifecycle methods. That gives you a smaller unit of caching for expensive, mostly static sections of a page.

Interactive Server apps can opt into automatic circuit pause when a browser tab becomes inactive. After a configurable delay, pausing frees the server memory and SignalR connection held by an inactive user. The feature requires an additional package and explicit configuration; upgrading doesn’t silently change your application’s circuit behavior.

Forms gain client-side validation for static server rendering and asynchronous validation support. and add ways to move to a particular item, useful when returning a user to their place in a large collection.

Blazor also adds components for agentic user interfaces. The new Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI package includes components for streaming chat, tool rendering, approval flows, and shared UI state. Basic chat works with any . For advanced experiences with a remote agent, the AG-UI .NET integration carries streamed responses, tool events, approval requests, and shared-state updates between an ASP.NET Core agent endpoint and the Blazor UI.

The Blazor AI components package is experimental and remains prerelease throughout .NET 11. It’s an opportunity to try the direction and give feedback, not a stable part of the ASP.NET Core shared framework. See the Blazor AI components documentation.

.NET MAUI in .NET 11 makes CoreCLR the default runtime across its platforms. The move to CoreCLR brings mobile and desktop apps onto the same runtime foundation as other .NET workloads. On Apple platforms that don’t allow JIT compilation, the runtime uses precompiled code and the interpreter rather than generating native code at runtime.

Native AOT is an opt-in publishing alternative; its Android support remains experimental. Review the platform-specific runtime guidance and test your app’s libraries when choosing a deployment model.

The UI development loop gets attention, too:

  • XAML Incremental Hot Reload is a in .NET 11. It updates live instances of pages and controls, including supported structural edits, without requiring you to navigate away and back. It’s enabled by default in Debug builds.
  • Implicit XAML namespace declarations remove the need to repeat the standard namespace declarations at the root of every file.
  • Windows uses the new handler by default, while Android Shell adopts a handler-based architecture.
  • New mobile test templates and device selection bring testing into the CLI workflow.

These are meaningful runtime and handler changes, so exercise navigation, custom handlers, and trimmed publishing as part of your upgrade. The optional Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships; apps that still reference it need to migrate off it.

.NET MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the .NET runtime’s STS and LTS lifecycle.

Windows: WinUI, Windows Forms, and WPF

For new Windows desktop apps, WinUI 3 is the recommended native UI framework, pairing C# and XAML with modern controls and the Fluent Design System. It’s delivered through the Windows App SDK, which also makes modern Windows APIs available to existing WPF and Windows Forms apps.

Windows Forms in .NET 11 adds an opt-in modern visual styles mode that you can select at the application or control level. It also adds ways to react to system visual and accessibility settings, defer revealing a form until it’s ready, and suspend painting during bulk updates.

These controls let you introduce refreshed rendering where it makes sense for your application instead of treating a framework upgrade as an automatic visual redesign.

WPF updates focus on reliability, including fixes for Fluent window backdrops, window manager failures, and weak-event cleanup. Self-contained Windows publishing also includes a native dependency needed by apps that load mixed-mode WPF assemblies.

Get started and plan your upgrade

To create and run a console app:

dotnet new console -n HelloDotnet11 -f net11.0
dotnet run --project HelloDotnet11

You can replace the generated program with either of the C# examples above to try the new language features.

For an existing application, plan the upgrade across your development and deployment environments:

  1. Update the SDK selection in if your repository pins it, and install the matching SDK on development machines and build agents.
  2. Update target frameworks to .NET 11, preserving platform-specific target framework suffixes where applicable. Update packages and workloads to compatible versions.
  3. Run your tests and measure the application under a representative workload. Validate your actual publishing mode, container base images, native dependencies, and deployment hosts.

Upgrading from .NET 8 or .NET 9

.NET 8 and .NET 9 reach end of support on November 10, 2026. Move to a supported release to continue receiving fixes. Choose .NET 11 for the latest capabilities, or .NET 10 if its LTS lifecycle fits your requirements better. See the .NET support policy for dates and servicing requirements.

If you’re upgrading from a .NET 11 release candidate, update to the final SDK, runtime, and compatible package and workload versions rather than staying on a prerelease build.

Thank you for building .NET with us

.NET 11 is the work of . Thank you to everyone who contributed code, tested previews, reported issues, and helped us make better design decisions throughout the year. Your feedback across the previews and release candidates helped shape what we’re shipping today.

The .NET ecosystem continues to grow, with more than on NuGet and over 1.1 trillion package downloads.

items.title: Horible public key tricks
items.author: Curiositry
items.content:
—

So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.

... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4"

of protest SSL implementations, but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.

The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be weak, no one would know unless they try to break it.

A good protest should be obvious: 

#  s_client -connect : < /dev/null 2>  \
    |  -n  |  -zE  --color=////You+dont+actually+have+to+pick+random+privat
e+keys//No+one+checks+these+things//A+certificate+authority+got+
away+with+the+number+4+for+a+year/////

First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent.

The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent: 

cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n

The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q. 

= cyphertext^d mod n

= plaintext^e^d mod n
= plaintext^(e*d) mod n
= plaintext^1 mod n
= plaintext

The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there.

The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus.

My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p.

The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product: 

58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176

58174124 * 9184918 = 5343245836

As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner.

From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key: 

 req -new  >  certonly --manual  > config req -new  >  certonly --manual
... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts.

The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated.

Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) available charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice.

, this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. However, it should still be secure: nearly identical methods have been considered as a form of compression. If the top-half of the modulus is fixed to a well known value, it doesn't have to be sent or stored as part of the key.

A reduction of around 1/2 can be achieved through division, but the state of the art can fix 2/3 of the key, reducing the size to 1/3 of standard RSA while retaining a similar level of security... although I should note that such tricks have largly been abandoned in favor of other crytosystems which can directly use small keys.

The manipulation of q may produce primes that are very close together, which makes it possible to factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also be a problem. Both of these are unlikely, but my script doesn't check for insecure values

However, regardless of the key's security, it should be perfectly fine for a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires a man-in-the-middle attack even if the private key is compromised.

items.content:
While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads.

The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements, our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry.

Building the computer around the chip

Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system.

Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases.

When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer, so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years.

items.title: The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford
items.author: edward
items.content:
Last week was fun. We launched tinylittleoffice.com—you heard it here first!—and it turned out that lots of folks were in the market for an “office suite that stores data in the URL.” 

So all good; we will continue to support and enhance it, bit by bit, while we also do stable software development work for our customers and clients. But I did want to pause for a second and point out something that surprised me about the process. It’s this:

The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for building applications.

I know that is obvious and is the sort of thing I could have said any time in the last 20 years. But now there’s an addendum to the statement: 

The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for applications, and the cost of accessing that power is going down seemingly every day.

I put maybe twice as much effort into building a web-based office suite as I might normally put into writing a long newsletter post. I’m not telling you this because I am a very special boy. I’m telling you because if you want to, you can learn to do it, too.

Fast, cheap, good, right? But even after I had to put in my credit card, CloudFlare hosting costs…$0. Partly because I optimize for cheapness, but partly because that’s just how it goes these days. Fast? Dear God, computers are fast, and software development is also fast compared to the past. But as I code web apps, I keep finding new corners of the browser I didn’t know well. Things are just…wild in there.

  • The Web Assembly platform lets you run native-speed code in your browser.
  • WebGL provides for high-quality 3D and 2D graphics in your browser.

And on and on. The web is really the greatest distribution platform imaginable right now. It’s inherently multilingual—I released TinyLittleOffice in 21 languages (the most common NYC ones, which is why it has Creole and Yiddish), with lots of infrastructure for accessibility. Plus, of course, JavaScript is a full-featured programming language, and HTML can represent most things a document can do on a computer; if you need something more old-school, PDF.js lets you deal with PDFs in the browser. I think you can even hyphenate text reliably these days, although I refuse to believe it.

I knew these things existed. I’d even programmed with them. But I’d never really looked closely; I just downloaded whatever open-source code would make it easier to build and tried to drag software across the finish line.

My quirky 1990s-vintage office suite might not convince you—it’s weird and small. So take a look at Simon Willison’s new web-based browser 3D game, Battle Drones. He’s hosting it on GitHub. He wrote it himself. He’s not a games builder. It just pops right up in the browser and you play it. It’s multiplayer, and it works offline.

… but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I’d love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!

All the various cool browser technologies have been around for years. But they are each extremely vast. If you get good at Web Audio, you probably don’t have time to get good at Web Crypto and Web Assembly and WebGL. 

The reason they were so complex is, basically, because they were built for teams like those at Google, not for individuals. In the past, the web was for people to build web pages—and, yes, in the present, you can still do that, but for more than a decade, the web has been designed for giant companies so they can deliver software securely to billions of people who buy things with credit cards. These huge mega-libraries were dropped into the web browser to enable large teams to build big things, and the little guy was a bit of an afterthought. But now you can make a game in 3D with sound, and it can work just fine on a plane.

This is one of the places where “are we in an AI bubble” gets fuzzy for me, because it’s totally clear all these giant AI companies are huffing AGI paint fumes, but at the same time, if we actually unlocked the economic transformation of, say, 100 times as many people making software for each other, that would blow an enormous crater into the current tech economy. Don’t like the way your giant industrial looms make carpet? Hack your own firmware and make each carpet totally personalized! Turn any Instagram post into a huge floor covering! Suddenly all the carpet companies have to hack their own firmware to compete. What’s that going to be like? 

This also destabilizes the app store economy. The high tax of building for app stores seems less worth paying when you can just test an idea in the world from a web server for $0 after a couple weeks. Perhaps Mozilla should take another swing at launching a mobile phone! (Forget I mentioned that.) In any case, what used to be a large industrial process is now a personal one, if you so desire. Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be.

It’s a mixed blessing. I’ve been a writer for years, and software development feels more and more like writing to me every passing week. The awkward part of the comparison is, in general, people do not want to pay writers any money at all. As a writer, you get used to it. But for software people, being perpetually devalued is pretty novel. Then again, if you need software to do something—like our clients!—say, to fix a process, organize a database, get more value out of a big piece of industrial equipment, it’s a pretty amazing time, because you can do just about anything. I’m pretty confident we’ll all meet in the middle, but it’ll take a while, and it will be different on the other side.

items.title: I'm not a fan of Deno's security model (2024)
items.author: maxloh
items.content:
(published on August 31, 2024)

this has been bothering me for a while now, so I want to write down my thoughts so I can get it out of my head and move on. we’re gonna talk about how Deno approaches security, specifically with its permissions system, and why I think this approach is fundamentally insecure and misleading.

Deno is a language runtime for JavaScript. it consists of a standard library, a package manager, a TypeScript transpiler and a bunch of other stuff that’s not important for our story. it’s not a JavaScript , so it does not interpret or compile JavaScript, it reuses V8 for that.

one of the flagship features of Deno is its permission system (it’s under the “Secure by default” header on their landing page). the idea is simple: as JS code running in Deno needs the standard library to access the outside world, Deno can choose which accesses it allows or disallows, so when you run

the standard library will only allow to read and run .

additionally, a program can request permissions at runtime, so code like

will display a nice little prompt in the terminal:

┌ ⚠️  Deno requests read access to "/tmp/dir".
├ Requested by `Deno.permissions.request()` API.
├ Run again with --allow-read to bypass this prompt.
└ Allow? [y/n/A] (y = yes, allow; n = no, deny; A = allow all read permissions) >

and you can grant or refuse it.

(aside: I really miss this feature in browser extensions. currently, if your extension needs access to website, it needs to request access to the websites, which is less than ideal)

if you like puzzles, this is the point where you can stop and think about what could go wrong with this system.

of the two specific issues I want to point out this is the less severe one. we’ll discuss it first because this was the first thing I noticed and it kinda immediately irked me when I first read about this.

(if you’re only interested in the more juicy part, you can skip to the next section).

so, this nice little prompt is displayed in the terminal. it’s not, like, a PolKit GUI window or anything, it’s just text on stdout waiting for input from stdin. this is a wild thing to do.

you see, terminal has a somewhat weird API. most of the commands / requests application can send to the terminal are sent in-band, by printing them to stdout. terminal can then reply by sending data to stdin. as Deno allows programs to print arbitrary data to stdout and read from stdin without requiring any permissions or doing any filtering, malicious code can send arbitrary commands to the terminal. it’s usually okay, because terminals won’t, like, execute shell commands just because stdout told them to, you’re supposed to be able to freely files without risking arbitrary code execution. it’s markedly less okay if you allow malicious code to do whatever with the terminal and then print a prompt on the same exact terminal.

you could, like, hide the prompt by messing with terminal colors. (this one got closed in 2026 because the permission prompt is “partially visible” (you can see an emoji) and “AI agents tend to” change terminal colors, so that’s a “valid use-case”)

the specific issue on the screencast is long patched; the issue with terminal colors is not. that doesn’t really matter because the issue is using an attacker-controlled channel for security-sensitive information. it’s like executing attacker-controlled JS code on a webpage and then asking for password on the same page. you can’t know that the page is in a safe state, so you can’t trust any input.

even if Deno manages to patch every single issue with the “standard” escape codes, you never know which non-standard codes even exist out there. many terminals have some, it’s impossible to predict how they will interact with your prompt.

(aside: how come sudo can do it then? the difference is that sudo asks for the password first, before running any other code. to trick sudo that way you’d need to fuck up terminal state before you even type , and do it quietly enough that you don’t notice it while you type it. if some terminal allows it, I’d consider it a bug in the terminal)

so, there’s a weird thing with this command I wrote above (I’ll copy it here for reference):

what does even mean? it’s not like programs have canonical names, it’s not , it’s not even /nix/store/8k1dmzr3gwzqdgw45nzj76902ca7g1is-coreutils-full-9.5/bin/uname. it’s just a shortcut for “look at all the directories in one-by-one to see if you can find there”.

you can set environment variables for the child process without needing any extra permissions, so what if we just

$ cat t.ts
const command = new Deno.Command("uname", {
  // my current working directory, can be anything
  env: { 'PATH': '/tmp/tmp.7ofmKaNW83' },
});
const { code, stdout, stderr } = command.outputSync();
console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(stdout));
$ cat uname
#!/bin/sh
printf lol
$ deno run --allow-run=uname t.ts
lol

once again, we have a pretty and convenient interface that doesn’t really make sense from the security standpoint. it would be if programs were uniquely identified by their names, but they’re , and pretending they are leads to security holes.

funnily enough, I didn’t even think that this issue would be there when I poked at Deno for the first time, so I haven’t reported it until now (spoiler alert: this is a comment on a GitHub issue that I created for the problem I’ll explain below).

so let’s imagine we fixed that. it’s not hard, we can force to be whatever it was when the runtime started, or always require fully-qualified paths, or prompt with a fully-qualified path before running. are we safe now?

lol no of course we’re not. while decides which executable gets run, dynamically-linked executables (so, like, most executables) require dynamic loader to actually start. dynamic loader is a program that, well, loads the executable into memory, finds its dependencies and does a bunch of other fun stuff we won’t get into. the important part is that dynamic loader is via environment variables. you can probably see where this is going now.

instructs the dynamic loader to load specific dynamic library when loading executables. dynamic libraries can execute arbitrary code on load. we can just pass and we’ve completely escaped the sandbox once again:

$ cat t.c
#include <stdio.h>

// ask dynamic loader to run this function on load time pretty please
__attribute__((constructor)) void lol() {
    puts("lol");
}
$ cat t.ts
const command = new Deno.Command("uname", {
  // ask dynamic loader to load our evil library
  env: { 'LD_PRELOAD': '/tmp/tmp.7ofmKaNW83/liblol.so' },
});
const { code, stdout, stderr } = command.outputSync();
console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(stdout));
$ gcc -fPIC -shared t.c -o liblol.so
$ # that's the real uname now!
$ deno run --allow-run=uname t.ts
lol
Linux

I reported this some time ago and now they patched it by disallowing to set environment variables starting with . this, once again, fixes a specific issue while ignoring the larger problem: “permission to run a single command” is mostly not a useful concept. (you do secure interfaces by allowing to run a single command, like git-over-SSH does, but generally both the environment and the command need to be prepared to handle it)

say, for example, our script wants to invoke the so user can edit some data (think git commit messages). that’s a very natural permission request, and it’s also an unmitigated disaster because most editors are configurable enough for running one to be a full sandbox escape. it’s easy for user to absent-mindedly grant (“well, sure, I want to edit this file!”), but then the script can just set and oops, all my files are gone. most programs are configurable, often in some ways you won’t think about (like ), and attacker controls the execution enviornment. “patch some specific ways to configure programs” is not the solution, the solution is to sandbox all the code, not just JS code.

when we discussed all this stuff in GitHub issues, a Deno developer wrote:

The main thing it protects you against is malicious code that isn't smart enough.

upon reading this, I was enlightened.

deno tries really hard to do what the operating system should be doing. it emulates syscall filtering by filtering standard library calls. unfortunately, this breaks down the second you need to run code that doesn’t use Deno standard library. it also uses somewhat flawed approach to permission management that good (wow, runtime prompts! omg, I can just !), but introduces security risks. in doing this, it implicitly requires user to understand all the implications of various permissions and their combinations, which can be really hard.

Deno process is not actually sandboxed, it only pretends it is. I didn’t mention some more boring issues like “Deno doesn’t prevent you from following symlinks that lead outside of the sandbox” because they all just boil down to this simple one: the process is not sandboxed.

one can argue that this pseudo-sandboxing is better than nothing: after all, not all the malicious code is smart enough. I disagree: Deno permissions give a false sense of security and can lure someone into running untrusted code without proper sandboxing.

it’s possible that you can use Deno sandboxing safely if you:

  • never use more dangerous permissions like , even with ,
  • that includes , even , for setting environment variables is memory unsafe and can affect libc functions,
  • preferrably run with so your terminal can’t be tricked,
  • are careful about symlinks in directories you to,
  • are not concerned with resource exhaustion: there’re zero permissions required to burn CPU or allocate memory.

in particular, you may be safe if you’re running untrusted code with no permissions at all in a non-interactive context and use some other mechanism to control resource consumption.

I still don’t think you do it. this path is riddled with footguns because you’re executing untrusted code in a fully-privileged process, and the moment you need OS interactions you’re no longer running code “with no permissions at all”. you should not try to figure out which stdlib APIs can lead to a sandbox escape when combined. you should just use a proper sandbox.

I’m not a fan of Deno’s security model.

also, please: don’t harass Deno developers. we have a technical disagreement, but no technical disagreement was ever solved by harassment. this post is explicitly not an invitation to do it. I’ve already explained my point of view to them, they disagreed, and that’s okay. you don’t need to reiterate it, it won’t help anybody.

items.title: JIT bitmap text rendering for microcontrollers
items.author: dmit
items.content:
Raph Levien, November 7, 2026

I've been working on vic-2350, a re-envisioning of an 80s home computer on an RP2350 microcontroller board. Of course, such a project needs text rendering. Though bitmap fonts are now out of favor, I chose them both for efficiency and because, at low resolutions, I prefer the aesthetic of a crisp, intentionally designed bitmap font over the blurry mush of antialiased font rendering. They still have a niche, if a narrow one.

I also wanted proportional spacing and kerning, again because I love the aesthetic of early Macintosh and its predecessors. Most text rendering in RP2350 projects is based on a fixed character cell, as achieving good performance is tricky.

This blog post presents a technique for extremely fast rendering of bitmap text on microcontrollers such as the RP2350. I've implemented it as part of my race-the-beam renderer, but the same technique would work when writing into a framebuffer as well. The core idea is a JIT to generate highly optimized code on the fly for rendering a string.

Around the mid-80s, a split was happening in the way computers displayed text. The established technique was a fixed cell size, and hardware that looked up characters in a font ROM on the fly as the image was scanned out to the monitor. The advantage was very fast update and responsiveness with limited hardware. A lot of terminals worked this way, as did home computers. The downside was the lack of flexibility. In particular, only monospace fonts were supported.

The newer technique was a bitmap framebuffer, as pioneered on a line of computers originating with the Xerox Alto, continuing through the Apple Lisa, and finally becoming popular with the Macintosh. The framebuffer was vastly more flexible, but required a lot more computing power to keep updated. In the early 80s, you would generally watch text progressively render. I should also mention, graphics modes were generally available on home computers, but they were typically lower resolution than text mode and a 1MHz 6502 (or similar) was just not powerful enough, so serious text-based programs like word processors and spreadsheets used text mode.

Fast forward to the RP2350. It is capable of DVI video out with the help of the HSTX peripheral, but it is still entirely up to software to fill the video buffer. Some projects choose a framebuffer, but there's only 520kB of SRAM on the chip, so a framebuffer must be limited in either resolution or bit depth or both, and it would also be good for that RAM to be available to the app for other purposes. I've chosen instead to race the beam, filling a video buffer each scanline. That allows more visual richness and much lower latency, but is a hard performance constraint on the renderer. There's a budget of approximately 6 cycles per pixel. The lower we come in under budget, the more is available for rendering other graphical objects, and for other app functions.

Rust is not capable of meeting the performance requirement, so I started writing ARM assembly language. The renderer, and much of vic-2350, is now written in symbolasm, a programming language I've created for extremely high performance Cortex-M33 programming. Employing a JIT speeds up rendering further.

Rendering is often modeled as a pipeline, and the vic-2350 renderer is no exception. The interface between application and renderer is a At heart, that's just what it says, a list of The display list is double-buffered; one is being rendered and scanned out, and the other is built by the application. At each vsync, if the app is ready, the display list is swapped. Building the display list is not computationally intensive, but of course the app might be busy doing other things.

As the display list is of unknown size at compile time, it allocates. Display objects are packed into two vectors; one holds the display objects themselves, the other a list of indices into the first vector. A display object consists of a vtable, a bounding rectangle, and the object-specific payload. Allocation is acceptable because the display list is not timing critical. Rendering is a different story. That said, it is important for the display list to be memory efficient, especially as there are two copies.

Before presenting, the indices are sorted into ascending y0 order.

During rendering, the renderer maintains an which is just the subset of display objects that intersect the current scanline. At each scanline, objects for which y1 = y are deleted from the active list, and new objects with y0 = y are inserted, which is the reason for the sort earlier; it is exactly the order objects are inserted into the active list. The active list is kept in display object order.

Then the renderer just calls the method for each display object in the active list. I'll do a bit more optimization soon, tracking opaque spans and eliding rendering work for spans of pixels that will be overwritten later, but that's not fundamental to the text rendering as presented here.

At the start and end of an object (when it's inserted and deleted) the renderer calls and methods on the display object. These methods can allocate scratch space and do other work to set up rendering of the object. There's a specialized bitmap allocator, which is both fast and deterministic.

All this gives us everything we need to implement text rendering as an instance of display objects.

The text object itself contains the string (1 byte per character), a pointer to the font, and foreground and background colors. RAM is precious, and more so for the display list because it's double buffered. In an earlier iteration of the renderer, I had an expanded version of the text stored in the display list, and that created unacceptable memory pressure when the screen was filled with text.

The method allocates scratch space for both the JIT code and a 1 bit per pixel intermediate buffer, and invokes the JIT compiler, expanding the string into code.

The method calls that code, which fills the 1 bit per pixel buffer, then runs a second pass to expand that 1 bit per pixel buffer into 16 bit per pixel RGB (565 format). This second pass runs at a sustained rate of 1.75 cycles per pixel.

The font is stored in extremely packed format. All the "ink" for glyphs is stored in a wide bitmap image, same height as the font. The packing also makes sure no glyph straddles a 32-pixel chunk boundary, so one row of font pixels can always be read with a single 32 bit load. If a glyph has space on either side of the glyph, that's not stored in the packed bitmap; rather, the space is in the per-glyph metadata.

In the spirit of micro-optimization, the packing algorithm also detects overlaps, as there's no requirement that pixels be unique to a single glyph. This optimization reduces the size of the font bitmap from 1140 to 960 bytes. Every byte counts, and more so as we add more fonts. The font bitmap needs to live in SRAM, as having it in flash could cause stalls during rendering at video rate.

I especially liked the sequence (near the start of the second row). Any glyph contained within another glyph doesn't need to be packed separately. There are a few examples, some surprising. For example, is the left side of , and is identical to with the space between them removed.

The per-glyph metadata (not counting kerning) is conceptually four fields: the x position and width of the ink within the bitmap, the space on the left, and the advance. All this is tightly packed into a 32 bit integer.

In the generated JIT code, registers are assigned as follows:

  • r0 points to the beginning of the row of the packed font bitmap
  • r1 is the output buffer, a one-line 1 bit per pixel image buffer
  • r2 is the accumulator for the output bitmap
  • r3 holds the bits of one glyph, extracted from r4
  • r4 holds 32 bits loaded from the glyph bitmap

In the simplest case, we add one glyph to the accumulator. The code looks like this:

There's additional code to output a word when it's finished (), and to handle cases when a glyph straddles a 32 bit boundary. These are documented in text.sy. But there is one trick I do want to mention here: the code as above has a result-use delay between the and (unsigned bit field extract). This is solved by shuffling the order of instructions somewhat: the last instruction for glyph is reordered to follow the first instruction () of glyph , filling the delay slot, and reducing the cycle cost from 4 to 3.

Here's the inner loop of the code generator, focusing only on the case where the glyph doesn't straddle the accumulator. For each glyph, several values are packed into the variable, then unpacked below: the offset within the packed font bitmap (which further breaks down into a bit offset and a word offset), the width of the inked part, the left side bearing, and the advance.

Here's the compiled ARM assembly code from the above symbolasm code, along with cycle count analysis from the symbolasm analysis tool:

The flags indicate a possible delay in branches because the condition isn't known until the cycle before the branch. Here, indicates 0 cycles if the branch is not taken, and 2 if it is. Neither of these can be optimized. The flag indicates the instruction is 32 bits rather than 16 because of the use of "hi" registers (r8-r15). These are available in the LSP as well.

Without a JIT, it would be possible to write text rendering as a loop, but in the proportionally spaced case, there'd be a huge amount of setup to work out the shift amounts, plus branching to handle cases like straddling a 32 bit boundary. Earlier implementations of the idea in pico-dvi-rs struggled to display a full screen of text. Of course, for fixed width text all that is known statically, so a tight loop without JIT is fine.

The basic loop is 23 cycles per glyph for the JIT plus 3 cycles times height for the bitmap generation. There's an additional cost of about 20 cycles for JIT and 2 cycles times height per 32 bits of output width.

This is astonishingly fast. The textdemo in vic-2350 takes about 21k cycles for the JIT and 42k cycles to run the JIT code. That adds up to about 2.6% of the available throughput of a single core of the RP2350. Expanding to 565 is actually about 3x more expensive. So it's fair to say it's as optimized as it can get.

While this was designed for race-the-beam rendering, it would work just as well writing into a framebuffer, especially a one bit per pixel framebuffer. Just generate the code, run it for each scanline.

It's tempting to cache the JIT output, but saving RAM is more important. The JIT output is about a 10x expansion over the input string. And, from the numbers above, it's clear that the cost of running the JIT is minimal.

The name "just in time" is apt; in the implementation in vic-2350, the JIT compiler runs under 100µs before scanout of the video line.

I wasn't able to find a direct performance comparison to an existing RP2350 text renderer. Probably the closest is dvhstx by Michael Bell and forked by Adafruit. That also ends up spending approximately 2-2.5 cycles total per pixel, but is limited to a 14x24 grid and also uses an RGB 222 mode, so its output bandwidth is only half as much (and this is where the lion's share of the time goes).

Kerning is a very important refinement for text rendering, otherwise the spacing looks irregular. The general mechanism in OpenType fonts is quite complex. For this project, I wanted something simple and efficient, so dusted off an idea that was originally motivated by trying to do text layout on GPU.

Basically, each glyph has two bitvectors, one each for the left and right side. To kern two glyphs, take the of the right bitvector of the first glyph and the left bitvector of the second, then the popcount (number of bits) of that, resulting in the number of pixels to kern. That's actually just the dot product of the two vectors, bits interpreted as 0 and 1. The kern tables require only two bytes per glyph, and kerning is super fast to evaluate.

Even so, kerning evaluation is done at display list build time, not racing the beam. When the kern is nonzero, a special negative space character is inserted into the string in the text display object.

For this font, I built the kerning table manually. Each bit is a specific feature, for example bit 0 represents the top right of the first glyph projecting out, and a corresponding lack of ink in the top left of the next glyph. So it is set for the right of and , and also at the left of most lowercase letters and also . It's not hard to imagine a tool that might help automate this, perhaps distilling kerning information prepared in other ways.

I haven't done a real implementation yet, but I suspect this idea might scale to real fonts: instead of bits and an integer kerning amount, the vectors would store continuous values (reasonably quantized). An additional nonlinear step after the multiplication but before the sum may also help. Dot products are of course ridiculously efficient to compute on GPU, while doing index chasing through OpenType tables is not. But that exploration is for another day.

Kerning improves quality considerably:

This work is a refinement of the text rendering in pico-dvi-rs, which was hand-written. My draft of the JIT core was hand-written in Rust, then I used Claude to translate it to symbolasm and refine and optimize it. This blog is hand-written.

The symbolasm compiler and analysis tool is heavily LLM assisted, though it too evolved from an initial hand-written version.

I did a microtypography experiment that was a pretty cool result, but decided not to include it, partially because it would have increased the fraction of LLM content.

Like most other people in the industry, I struggle with the balance between quality and the acceleration that LLMs provide. Claude is exceedingly good at the low level tasks of coding; it easily found an edge case in my draft of the JIT compiler. I find that when used judiciously, LLM can improve quality, and I strive for that.

I wasn't able to find much precedent for JIT specifically for text rendering. Of course, there is a massive literature on JIT in general. On-the-fly code generation for bitblt was done for the Blit around 1982. See Bitmap Graphics SIGGRAPH 84 for more. An interesting detail is that they claim about 2500 characters per second; the raw performance of this on RP2350 hardware is almost 3 orders of magnitude greater, just counting the output to 1bpp (which is how the Blit's framebuffer was configured).

Edit added later: David Fuchs pointed out [US Patent 6377261], filed in 1996, which compiled glyphs to machine code. It's highly optimized for speed, and has a lot in common with the idea here, but depends on a cache to be reasonably RAM efficient. Even so, it absolutely counts as prior art.

items.title: Simon Winchester has died
items.author: benbreen
items.content:
Simon Winchester, a British-American journalist, author and broadcaster, who traded an early career as a geologist exploring East Africa for an even more peripatetic résumé covering stories from Northern Ireland’s bloodstained Troubles to Watergate-era Washington, the Falklands war and China, died on Tuesday on his farm in Sandisfield, Mass., according to his wife, Setsuko Winchester. He was 82.

The cause of death was a heart attack, she said.

His reporting days were studded with adventure and peril. During the Argentine invasion of the Falkland Islands and Britain’s reconquest of the remote, Atlantic territory in 1982, he achieved twin distinctions of being on the islands when they were first occupied, then being arrested in southern Patagonia, mistaken for a spy, and imprisoned for three months, according to a biography on his website.

Mr. Winchester made the switch from geology to journalism after reading “Coronation Everest,” a book about the 1953 first ascent of Mount Everest, by Jan Morris, then known as James Morris, who had covered the momentous expedition.

Mr. Winchester read the book while encamped in Uganda’s Rwenzori Mountains and resolved to become a reporter himself, writing to Ms. Morris to seek advice. She replied that, if he wanted to join the ranks of traveling writers, his best course would be to return to England and work on a newspaper. He duly began his own ascent on the profession’s heights not in the Himalayas but in Newcastle-upon-Tyne in northeast England.

items.title: Five memorable books about programming (2008)
items.author: andsoitis
items.content:
I've read the classics--Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, Paradigms of Artificial Intelligence Programming--but I'd like to highlight some of the more esoteric books which affected my thinking.

Michael Abrash, 1990

I spent much of the 1980s writing 8-bit computer games (which you can read about if you like). Odd as it may seem in retrospect, considering the relative power of an 8-bit 6502 running at sub 2 MHz, I wasn't obsessed with optimizing for performance. If anything, I wanted the code to be , a side effect of using a line-based editor and writing programs that someone would have to painstakingly type in from a magazine listing. Pages of DATA 0AFF6CA900004021... ugh.

Right when that period of my life came to a close, along came , by an author I had never heard of, which dissected, explained, and extended the self-taught tricks from my years as a lone assembly hacker. Even though Abrash was focused on the 8086 and not the 6502, it felt like the book was written personally to me.

This is also one of the most bizarrely delayed technical book releases I can recall. The majority of the book was about detailed optimization for the 8088 and 8086, yet it was published when the 80486 was showing up in high-end desktop PCs.

Julian Noble, 1992Fractals, Visualization, and J Clifford Reiter, 2000

These two books are about entirely different subjects. One is about pure scientific computation. The other is about generating images. Each uses a different, wildly non-mainstream language for the included code.

And yet these two books follow the same general approach, one I wish were more commonly used. Superficially, the authors have written introductions to particular programming languages (which is why the language name is in the title). But in reality it's more that each author has an area of deep expertise and has found a language that enables experimenting with and writing code to solve problems in that field. As such, there aren't forced examples and toy problems, but serious, non-trivial programs that show a language in actual use. Dr. Noble demonstrates how he uses Forth for hardcore matrix work and, when he realizes that RPN notation isn't ideal in all circumstances, develops a translator from infix expressions to Forth. Clifford Reiter jumps into image processing algorithms, plus veers into lighter weight diversions with titles like "R/S Analysis, the Hurst Exponent, and Sunspots."

Both books are wonderful alternatives to the usual "Learning Programing Language of the Month" texts. Sadly, Julian Noble died in 2007.

Susan Lammers, 1986

I used to soak up printed interviews with programmers and game designers (and typically game designers were programmers as well). I was enthralled by Levy's , more the game development chapter than the rest. was in the same vein: philosophies, ideas, and experiences directly from an odd mix of famous and quirky programmers. But the book wasn't primarily about tech. It was about creativity. Most of the people interviewed didn't have degrees in computer science. There wasn't an emphasis on math, proving programs correct, lambda calculus--just people coming up with ideas and implementing them. And the game connection was there: Jaron Lanier talking about the psychedelic for the Commodore 64, Bill Budge's bold (and still unfulfilled) plan to build a "Construction Set Construction Set."

Lammers's book was the model I used when I put together Halcyon Days. I also pulled into the mix by interviewing John Harris about his dissatisfaction with Levy's presentation of him. In an odd twist of fate, and were packaged together on a single CD sold through the Dr. Dobb's Journal library. The pairing has been around for ten years and is still available, much to my surprise.

Yes, another book about Forth.

But this one is worth reading less for the Forth and more because it's one of the few books about how to decompose problems and structure code. You'd think this book was written by Fowler and friends, until you realize it's from the mid-1980s. That Brodie uses "factor" (which originated in the Forth community) instead of "refactor" is also a giveaway. What's impressive here is there's no OOP, no discussion of patterns, no heavy terminology. It's a book about understanding what you're trying to achieve, avoiding redundancy, and writing dead simple code.

It's worth it for the Forth, too, especially the interspersed bits of wisdom from experts, including Forth creator Chuck Moore.

items.title: Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign
items.author: fiej
items.content:
When customers order food online, they expect a familiar experience: find their restaurant, choose their meal, and pay. Increasingly, criminals are exploiting that familiarity by creating convincing clones of restaurant ordering websites, right down to the original site's underlying code.

In early November 2026, InfoHawk researchers investigated a collection of suspicious websites that appear to be part of one or more coordinated restaurant impersonation and payment-skimming operations.

Across two research passes, we identified 820 domains impersonating 35 restaurant brands. Of those, 808 use the top-level domain, and the rest use or .

The scale is concerning, but what makes these sites particularly dangerous is how convincing they can be.

These aren't ordinary fake websites

The investigation began with a suspicious domain: mlckessejersstey[.]delivery.

The site impersonated Jersey Mike's, the popular sandwich chain, and reproduced its online ordering experience.

Rather than simply displaying a crude imitation of the restaurant's website, the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious one.

A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.

In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.

This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's bank uses that code.

For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears at the moment a customer expects to pay.

Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content they display.

Each clone is a : a server that sits between the victim and the real restaurant site, fetches every page from the real site as it is requested, edits it on the way through, and passes it on. Menus, prices, store hours, and the cart are live and correct, because they come from the real site. Only the payment step is replaced. Described from mlckessejersstey[.]delivery (Jersey Mike's); we believe the clones of the other brands run the same kit.

  1. The victim arrives from a search ad

    A Google Search ad imitates the restaurant's listing and shows a look-alike domain. The domain is behind Cloudflare, so its real server is hidden, and Cloudflare gives it a valid certificate automatically (Google Trust Services here), so the browser shows "Connection is secure".

  2. Every page is fetched live from the real site

    The proxy forwards each request to the restaurant's own servers, adjusting the host name and cookies, and relays the answer. The real site's headers come through (on Jersey Mike's, and Amazon CloudFront headers), which is how we could tell which paths came from the real site and which from the scammer's server.

  3. Addresses are rewritten to keep the victim on the fake domain

    The proxy replaces the brand's own host names in pages, scripts, and redirects with the fake domain, and maps each backend to a path on it, such as or . Store lookup, menus, login, and cart all work, because those calls go back through the proxy to the real APIs. Even the brand's own bot-detection script still runs, with its endpoints rewritten.

  4. Three scripts are injected into every page

    patches HTMLScriptElement.prototype.src so that listed scripts never load (on Jersey Mike's, the OneTrust cookie banner and Branch, which could send phone users to the app or the real domain). finds the real checkout payment frame and points it at on the fake domain; a MutationObserver puts the fake one back whenever the page restores the real one. reads the order total from the "Place order" button every half second and saves it, so the fake form shows the right amount.

  5. The card form is the scammer's

    A few paths are answered by the scammer's server instead of the real site: (the card form and its scripts) and . The form looks like part of checkout. On submit it collects every field (card number, expiry, CVV, name, phone) and sends it, with the site name, to the operator over a live socket.io connection.

  6. An operator gets past the bank's check live

    We believe a person watching a control panel uses the card elsewhere and, when the bank challenges that payment, tells the victim's page what to show next: "card declined, try another", a page asking for the SMS code (), an "approve in your bank app" page (), or "invalid code, try again". We believe the code the victim types is what lets the operator's charge through 3-D Secure.

  7. When the operator marks it a success, the page sets a cookie lasting until 2038 and sends the victim to another chain's real site (href.li/?https://www.jimmyjohns.com/; href.li hides where they came from). No order reaches the restaurant: the real payment step never runs, so there is no confirmation email and no food. We believe the victim's card is then charged for whatever the operator bought.

The clone never goes out of date, the victim builds a real order with a real total before anything looks wrong, and one kit works against any restaurant by changing the target site, the domain, and a few path rules. The scammer's server does very little work, which makes it cheap to move. Some variants skip the payment wording and only pin the frame's address, re-setting it every time the page changes it.

Most of the clones sit behind Cloudflare (AS13335), which hides the real servers: 761 of the 820 domains use Cloudflare nameservers, 11 use other nameservers, and 48 have none. Another cluster of 68 domains is tied to an Amazon Web Services (AWS) server. Some of its sites are served straight from that server, in Frankfurt () through nameservers, and its pages carry a different injected script (). It uses the same cloning technique, but we found nothing that shows the same people run it, so these sites may come from more than one operator using the same kit.

In our first sweep of 255 domains, 251 were registered at Dynadot, spread across 111 Cloudflare nameserver pairs.

What this means for restaurant brands

These clones don't need to break into a restaurant's systems. They borrow the real site, page by page, and insert the attack only at the moment a customer pays. That makes them hard to spot from the outside, but it also means the brand's own servers see every page the clone serves. Brands and their ordering providers that watch for their site loading under someone else's domain, or for checkout sessions that never reach the real payment provider, are well placed to catch these sites early.
